879a29f4908950e9c42ee446.title: Charity campaigner who died after microlight crash was filming Apple TV series, inquest hears
879a29f4908950e9c42ee446.author: Raphael Boyd
879a29f4908950e9c42ee446.content:
A disability campaigner who was paralysed from the chest down died after her microlight crashed while filming a TV series for Apple, an inquest has heard.
Claire Lomas, 44, who was the first person to complete a marathon with the help of a “bionic” suit, died five weeks after the adapted aircraft she was travelling in “veered off the runway” and hit a large rock while landing in Amman, Jordan.
The mother of two had become a noted campaigner for disability charities after a horse riding accident in 2007 left her paralysed.
Louise Pinder, senior coroner for Rutland and North Leicestershire, told the inquest on Tuesday that Lomas suffered multiple severe traumatic injuries during the crash on 15 July and was taken to King Hussein medical centre, where she died on 22 August.
The hearing, which took place at County Hall in Glenfield, Leicester, heard that at the time of her accident, Lomas had been wearing an Apple Vision Pro headset and was in the process of filming content for the tech company to be used in a series promoting the product.
![Claire Lomas crosses the finishing line held by a Cockney pearly king and queen. She is wearing a bionic suit and on crutches.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/dcef5fbeee5c190e79f283ff5dfe751e568d0a4f/0_0_3540_2204/master/3540.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Lina Zilinskaite, a senior producer for Atlantic Productions, told the inquest that Apple had commissioned her company to create the series, and Lomas was one of several athletes selected to perform “some sort of challenge or feat” in different episodes.
Zilinskaite told the court that Lomas had been “very enthusiastic and keen and excited about the opportunity” and that she had obtained a licence to fly a microlight, the small aircraft she was piloting at the time of the crash, years before the series was commissioned.
This was supported by Ben Ashman, a microlight designer and manufacturer, who said that Lomas had bought her own version of the aircraft between 2022 and 2023, which had been adapted to support her inability to use her feet.
Speaking on the events leading up to the crash, Zilinskaite told the hearing that Lomas’ flight had been scheduled for the day before but was cancelled “because of strong winds”. Zilinskaite also said that there had been test flights using the Vision Pro in the UK without Lomas, and that she had flown the microlight herself before the accident, albeit without wearing the headset.
On the day of the flight, the inquest was told that Lomas had taken off from the runway in Jordan without issue and remained in the air for roughly 15 minutes before attempting to land, but that upon descending her “approach was not quite straight on” and that she “veered off the runway” before striking a large rock.
The inquest heard that Lomas, who had completed the London Marathon over the course of 17 days in 2012 with the assistance of “bionic” legs, had been “excited” to return to the UK after the crash and see her family, but that her health rapidly deteriorated after catching an infection which led to her death.
Pinder said Lomas’ family had raised concerns about the quality of care in the Jordanian hospital, but that it was not within her jurisdiction to investigate that formally.
The inquest continues.
879a29f4908950e9c42ee446.summary: Disability campaigner Claire Lomas died from severe injuries five weeks after her adapted microlight crashed while landing in Amman, Jordan. Lomas, who was paralyzed after a 2007 horse riding accident and famously completed a marathon in a bionic suit, was filming a promotional series for Apple while wearing an Apple Vision Pro headset. The inquest heard that her aircraft veered off the runway and struck a rock, and her health subsequently deteriorated after she contracted an infection in the hospital.
key_points: Claire Lomas died on August 22 from multiple severe traumatic injuries following a microlight crash in Amman, Jordan, on July 15.
At the time of the accident, Lomas was filming content for an Apple TV series promoting the Apple Vision Pro headset.
Lomas had previously become well-known as a disability campaigner after completing the 2012 London Marathon using a bionic suit.
During the landing, her adapted aircraft veered off the runway and hit a large rock.
Her health rapidly deteriorated after she contracted an infection following the crash.

8a66aebdb8152493a12ee570.title: Wladimir Klitschko pays tribute to ex-partner Hayden Panettiere: ‘She left this world too soon’
8a66aebdb8152493a12ee570.author: Richard Luscombe
8a66aebdb8152493a12ee570.content:
Hayden Panettiere’s daughter will be raised to remember her mother’s “immense talent” and “incredible career”, according to a tribute posted on social media on Tuesday by Wladimir Klitschko, the ex-lineal world heavyweight boxing champion and the late Hollywood actor’s former partner.
Their daughter, Kaya, has been raised by the Ukrainian retired world boxing champion since 2018, when Panettiere ceded full custody to concentrate on her battles with alcoholism, depression and substance abuse.
Her death in Greenville, South Carolina, was reported on Sunday, with no cause given.
“Our family is going through a time of profound shock and grief,” Klitschko wrote in the Instagram post, which featured a photograph of himself and Panettiere smiling at a beach, with Kaya – whose face is obscured – perched on her mother’s shoulders.
“The announcement of Hayden’s tragic death saddens me deeply. She left this world far too soon. Hayden was, although no longer my partner, an important part of my life and the mother of our daughter, Kaya.”
The message also referenced the troubles that the Nashville and Heroes actor had experienced at a young age, following a succession of child stars who faced later challenges or tragedy.
“She built an incredible career through immense talent, while also facing the darker sides of a very demanding industry,” Klitschko wrote of Panettiere. “Nothing will erase the times we shared or the place she had in our lives.
“To our daughter Kaya, I will always speak of her mother with respect and make sure she remembers the person she was.”
Klitschko also sent his condolences to Panettiere’s grieving parents, friends and fans.
“Young and talented people like Hayden should not leave this world so soon,” he wrote. “I ask everyone to please respect our family’s feelings and privacy during this incredibly difficult time. For now, this is all I wish to say.
“Rest easy, Hayden. May you find eternal peace.”
In May, Panettiere expressed hope that she would one day be reunited with her daughter, who was born in 2014.
“I will always want her here. I always miss her,” she told podcaster Jay Shetty in an emotional interview.
“I always want to have my arms wrapped around her, but that’s just not the way life is right at this moment … I have faith that she is going to come to me and that we’re going to have an incredible relationship and bond and friendship that a lot of parents don’t get to have with their kids.”
Klitschko and Panettiere met at a book launch party in 2009, when the actor, then aged 20, was already a television star for her appearances as fictional high school cheerleader Claire Bennet in Heroes. After first splitting in 2011, they remained close friends and became engaged in 2013. Panettiere gave birth to Kaya a year later.
The actor struggled with postpartum depression, and the couple split for good in 2018, with Kaya spending time with her father at residences in Florida and Europe, E! News reported at the time.
8a66aebdb8152493a12ee570.summary: Former heavyweight boxing champion Wladimir Klitschko has paid tribute to his late former partner, actor Hayden Panettiere, following her death in South Carolina. In an Instagram post, Klitschko expressed profound grief and promised to ensure their daughter, Kaya, remembers her mother's talent and career. Panettiere, who shared a daughter with Klitschko born in 2014, had previously faced well-documented struggles with substance abuse, depression, and alcoholism, leading her to cede full custody of Kaya to Klitschko in 2018.

66ada5bfb1915e5892f0d33e.title: England vs Pakistan: A huge challenge, but Joe Root can finish captaincy story
66ada5bfb1915e5892f0d33e.author: Stephan Shemilt
66ada5bfb1915e5892f0d33e.content:
![England captain Joe Root trains at Headingley](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/c83b/live/dbff93c0-9b1e-11f1-a8a4-83462463c9fa.jpg)
Returning captain Joe Root has already led in 65 Tests, an England record
- Published
Of all the places for England to begin a new era, Headingley is the most difficult to shake off the memory of Ben Stokes.
In the city of Stokes' greatest miracle, the home side must plot a future without a captain, all-rounder and talisman, starting against Pakistan on Wednesday.
Yet, for all Stokes' legendary achievements it cannot be said his four-year spell as England captain ended with the team in a better state than he found it.
Stokes inherited a team that had won only one in 17 and exited with two wins in 10. New, old skipper Joe Root might wonder about the chaos his old mucker has left behind.
England have sacked Brendon McCullum as Test coach and replaced him with Stephen Fleming, only Fleming is not yet in post, meaning Marcus Trescothick is interim boss, all while McCullum remains floating around as white-ball gaffer.
It leaves this three-match series against Pakistan with a feeling of impermanence, not unlike Root's last tour as captain in the West Indies in 2022. England lost 1-0 with Paul Collingwood as temporary coach and Root resigned as captain soon after.
Root was left broken by his first, five-year, stint in the top job. There was a time when he would not have considered returning as skipper. Still, here he is on his home ground, ready to go again, smiling, excited and energised by his comeback.
Plenty will wonder why he wants to put himself through it all once more. Well, consider what it must be like to give up the England captaincy, to admit you can no longer do a dream job.
Root will have regrets from his first attempt, and maybe a sense of unresolved business. How irresistible it must be to get a second chance that very few are afforded.
If we thought Stokes' destiny was to end with an Ashes win next summer, then the all-rounder was unable to finish his story. Now Root has the opportunity to finish his.
The Yorkshireman has acknowledged one challenge of this captaincy is how some may view his first reign. Root was regularly self-deprecating about his own leadership during Stokes' tenure.
Yes, there was the one win in 17 to end it all, but before that, Root's record was pretty good: 26 wins from his first 47 matches in charge gave a success rate of 55%. As a comparison, Stokes won 54% of his Tests as skipper, Michael Vaughan 51% and Mike Brearley 58%.
How do England move on from Stokes?
Covid destroyed Root's team, and there are other reasons why Root might also feel he didn't get a fair shake first time around. His tenure as captain coincided with a prioritisation of white-ball cricket and, when he stood in for Stokes against New Zealand in June, he admitted to some envy at not getting the chance to work alongside McCullum.
Not that everything went against Root. One could argue that, given the players at his disposal, he should have had a better record as captain.
Peak Stokes, England's two greatest bowlers in James Anderson and Stuart Broad, plus the luxury of further all-rounders Chris Woakes and Moeen Ali. Root did not get to lead the best version of Alastair Cook, but the late-career Sir Chef would improve the current England team.
Root may feel he is better placed to captain England now, yet he is taking over if not a worse, then certainly a much more inexperienced team. Perhaps he will find this group easier to mould in his image. In his first Test as captain, in 2017, Root was the third-youngest player in the XI. In 2026, at the age of 35, he is comfortably the oldest.
For plenty of supporters the main worry will be the possibility of a detrimental effect the captaincy could have on Root's batting, and it is true that his average with the armband - 46.7 - is some way off a lofty 53.3 without.
That discrepancy is mainly because of a poor run in the middle of his first stint as skipper. Root averaged 37 in 2019, the year before things started going wrong for England during Covid.
In 2021, mid-pandemic and with the team falling apart, Root racked up 1,708 runs - the most by any England batter in a calendar year. He later explained that batting, being in the middle, was the only time he got any peace.
Root remains England's best player. Since the beginning of the Bazball era, he has scored almost 1,000 more Test runs than any other batter in the world. In the same period, he has moved second on the all-time list of run-scorers, with Sachin Tendulkar now in his sights.
Catchin' Sachin is the sub-plot to Root's second stint as captain, and he is adamant he can juggle the jobs of leadership and run-scoring.
England v Pakistan
First Test, Headingley
19-23 August, 11:00 BST
Ball-by-ball commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra and BBC Sounds. Live text updates, radio commentary and in-play video clips on the BBC Sport website and app. Today at the Test on BBC Two (BBC Four on 21 Aug) and BBC iPlayer from 19:00 BST.
His job as a leader will be to mould a group of players whose education in Test cricket was hampered by the informal approach of Stokes and McCullum. That point about Stokes not leaving the England squad in a better place than he found it? Root's team have questions about an opener and wicketkeeper, a makeshift number three, no obvious all-round option and are without a world-class spinner.
England start as favourites against a Pakistan team that has not won a series in this country in 30 years and will be without their own captain in Leeds, the injured Babar Azam.
Pakistan have, however, played more Tests in July and August than England â a 1-1 draw against West Indies. In seamer Mohammad Abbas and spinner Sajid Khan, they have bowlers who have caused England trouble in the past. If the tourists can get enough runs, it will be a competitive series.
After this, it gets very difficult for England. The winter includes trips to South Africa and Bangladesh, and a one-off pink-ball shootout against Australia.
Speaking of the Aussies, they will surely be better than they showed in defeat by Bangladesh when they arrive for the Ashes next summer. After that, England go to India in early 2028. It all adds up to a devilishly difficult first 18 months of Root's second tenure.
For all his runs, records, and milestones, perhaps rebuilding this England team in the face of the tasks ahead represents one of the greatest challenges of his storied career.
On top of that, Root has acknowledged the work his team have to do to rebuild their reputation with the public after a string of off-field misdemeanours. "Be good role models and good human beings," he has said to his players.
They should look no further than their captain for an example, for Root is one of the best.
66ada5bfb1915e5892f0d33e.summary: Joe Root has returned for a second stint as England's Test captain, starting with a three-match series against Pakistan at Headingley. He takes over a team left in a chaotic and inexperienced state following the departures of Ben Stokes and coach Brendon McCullum. Despite concerns over his batting average while captaining and the tough fixtures ahead, Root is energized and aims to finish his leadership story while chasing Sachin Tendulkar's run-scoring record.
key_points: Joe Root returns as England men's Test captain for a second stint, having previously led the team in a record 65 Tests.
England faces Pakistan in a three-match series at Headingley under interim coach Marcus Trescothick, following the exits of Ben Stokes and Brendon McCullum.
Root takes over a younger, more inexperienced squad facing a challenging schedule that includes upcoming tours to South Africa, Bangladesh, and Australia.
At 35 years old, Root is England's oldest player and aims to balance leadership duties while pursuing Sachin Tendulkar's all-time run-scoring record.

That discrepancy is mainly because of a poor run in the middle of his first stint as skipper. Root averaged 37 in 2019, the year before things started going wrong for England during Covid.
In 2021, mid-pandemic and with the team falling apart, Root racked up 1,708 runs - the most by any England batter in a calendar year. He later explained that batting, being in the middle, was the only time he got any peace.
Root remains England's best player. Since the beginning of the Bazball era, he has scored almost 1,000 more Test runs than any other batter in the world. In the same period, he has moved second on the all-time list of run-scorers, with Sachin Tendulkar now in his sights.
Catchin' Sachin is the sub-plot to Root's second stint as captain, and he is adamant he can juggle the jobs of leadership and run-scoring.
England v Pakistan
First Test, Headingley
19-23 August, 11:00 BST
Ball-by-ball commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra and BBC Sounds. Live text updates, radio commentary and in-play video clips on the BBC Sport website and app. Today at the Test on BBC Two (BBC Four on 21 Aug) and BBC iPlayer from 19:00 BST.
His job as a leader will be to mould a group of players whose education in Test cricket was hampered by the informal approach of Stokes and McCullum. That point about Stokes not leaving the England squad in a better place than he found it? Root's team have questions about an opener and wicketkeeper, a makeshift number three, no obvious all-round option and are without a world-class spinner.
England start as favourites against a Pakistan team that has not won a series in this country in 30 years and will be without their own captain in Leeds, the injured Babar Azam.
Pakistan have, however, played more Tests in July and August than England â a 1-1 draw against West Indies. In seamer Mohammad Abbas and spinner Sajid Khan, they have bowlers who have caused England trouble in the past. If the tourists can get enough runs, it will be a competitive series.
After this, it gets very difficult for England. The winter includes trips to South Africa and Bangladesh, and a one-off pink-ball shootout against Australia.
Speaking of the Aussies, they will surely be better than they showed in defeat by Bangladesh when they arrive for the Ashes next summer. After that, England go to India in early 2028. It all adds up to a devilishly difficult first 18 months of Root's second tenure.
For all his runs, records, and milestones, perhaps rebuilding this England team in the face of the tasks ahead represents one of the greatest challenges of his storied career.
On top of that, Root has acknowledged the work his team have to do to rebuild their reputation with the public after a string of off-field misdemeanours. "Be good role models and good human beings," he has said to his players.
They should look no further than their captain for an example, for Root is one of the best.
dd56a3897a635686f901e90d.summary: Joe Root has returned for a second stint as England's Test captain, starting with a three-match series against Pakistan at Headingley. He takes over a team left in a chaotic and inexperienced state following the departures of Ben Stokes and coach Brendon McCullum. Despite concerns over his batting average while captaining and the tough fixtures ahead, Root is energized and aims to finish his leadership story while chasing Sachin Tendulkar's run-scoring record.
key_points: Joe Root returns as England men's Test captain for a second stint, having previously led the team in a record 65 Tests.
England faces Pakistan in a three-match series at Headingley under interim coach Marcus Trescothick, following the exits of Ben Stokes and Brendon McCullum.
Root takes over a younger, more inexperienced squad facing a challenging schedule that includes upcoming tours to South Africa, Bangladesh, and Australia.
At 35 years old, Root is England's oldest player and aims to balance leadership duties while pursuing Sachin Tendulkar's all-time run-scoring record.

b84b561bac4cfbcb0c86dfbb.title: On 13 April 2029, a roughly 375-metre asteroid named Apophis will pass closer to Earth than some of our own satellites — just 32,000 kilometres above the surface — and new calculations suggest up to 90% of humanity could potentially see it cross the sky with the naked eye.
b84b561bac4cfbcb0c86dfbb.author: Space Daily; Deep Field
b84b561bac4cfbcb0c86dfbb.content:
On 13 April 2029, asteroid 99942 Apophis will pass roughly 32,000 kilometres above Earth’s surface. For a few hours it will be closer than satellites in geostationary orbit, bright enough to see without a telescope, and moving fast enough for its progress against the stars to become apparent.
The encounter is safe. NASA and ESA have ruled out an Apophis impact for at least the next century. A newer question is how much of humanity could stand outside and watch it happen.
Visibility maps presented in June 2026 put the potential audience as high as 7.6 billion people, close to 90 per cent of the world’s population. It describes people living somewhere inside the cumulative viewing region, not those sharing one clear view at the same moment.
The estimate came from a workshop presentation
Astrocartographer Michael Zeiler and astronomer Richard Tresch Fienberg presented the work at the Apophis T-3 Years workshop at the University of Padua on 18 and 19 June 2026. It was a conference presentation, not a peer-reviewed paper. The meeting covered modelling, missions, observations and public communication.
The maps begin with Apophis’s calculated trajectory. For each moment, the geometry determines where the asteroid is above the local horizon, whether the Sun is far enough below it and whether Apophis should be bright enough for unaided vision. A population layer then estimates how many people live in those changing regions.
According to reporting on Zeiler and Fienberg’s presentation, about 7.6 billion people fall somewhere within the cumulative footprint. The window lasts roughly seven hours, beginning near Australia and Asia around 15:00 UTC and ending over the North Atlantic near 22:00 UTC.
Cumulative does a great deal of work here. Australia, Asia, Africa, Europe and parts of eastern South America enter the useful viewing geometry at different times. The calculation does not put 90 per cent of humanity under the same night sky simultaneously, and North America is poorly placed for an unaided view.
Geometry is not a guarantee of clear skies
The calculation says where seeing Apophis should be possible. It cannot forecast local cloud, haze or how much city lighting will wash out the stars. Buildings, trees and terrain will remove more sightlines. Many people will simply not be looking.
Even under good conditions, Apophis will not resemble a meteor. It will not enter the atmosphere or trail fire. To the naked eye it should look like a modest star moving steadily across the background.
Fienberg’s observing preview for Sky & Telescope puts its peak near magnitude 2.8, comparable to an ordinary visible star. At that time, it may cross about 30 degrees of sky per hour, rising above 45 degrees per hour near closest approach. The Moon will be new, so moonlight should not interfere.
Peak brightness is expected around 20:35 UTC. Closest approach comes about an hour later. Those moments differ because the fraction of Apophis’s sunlit side facing Earth changes as it passes, so decreasing distance does not keep making it brighter.
Why Apophis has more than one quoted size
ESA calls Apophis roughly 375 metres across. NASA lists a mean diameter of about 340 metres and a long axis of at least 450 metres. The figures are not evidence that the asteroid has grown or that its size is unknown by a hundred metres. Apophis is elongated and irregular, so a mean diameter, an approximate overall size and its longest dimension answer slightly different questions.
The distance comparison also needs care. Geostationary satellites orbit about 35,786 kilometres above the equator. Apophis will come closer to the surface than that, but many other satellites fly hundreds or thousands of kilometres up and will remain far beneath it.
Nor is the asteroid travelling around the equatorial geostationary ring. It cuts across near-Earth space on a different path. NASA’s current overview says the flyby poses no danger to satellites, astronauts or anyone on Earth. “Closer than some satellites” describes altitude; it does not describe a collision course through a belt of spacecraft.
The same radar that removed the danger enabled the map
When Apophis was discovered in 2004, limited observations briefly left Earth inside part of the possible-orbit region. Further telescope data removed the 2029 impact route, but a small possibility in 2068 persisted because the close encounter will substantially alter the asteroid’s orbit.
That residual concern ended after Goldstone and Green Bank radar observations in March 2021. The radar images themselves are only a few bright pixels, recorded when Apophis was 17 million kilometres away. Precise echo timing mattered more than visual detail: it tightened the orbit enough for NASA to rule out impact for at least 100 years and remove Apophis from the Sentry risk table.
SpaceDaily recently told the longer story of that changing risk and the spacecraft preparing for 2029. The visibility work rests on the same achievement. The orbit is now constrained well enough to map not merely a safe miss, but the movement of a naked-eye point of light across local horizons.
What 90 per cent should mean by 2029
The maps will improve as new observations refine the trajectory and local viewing predictions. Weather forecasts will not become useful until much closer to the date. By then, city-specific charts should show where and when to look, while binoculars may rescue the view where light pollution makes naked-eye detection difficult.
The eventual audience will be smaller than 7.6 billion. The 90 per cent figure describes access in principle, subject to darkness, altitude, cloud, artificial light and attention. It is not a forecast of participation.
That distinction does not make the event ordinary. A safely passing asteroid a few hundred metres wide will move through naked-eye range over some of Earth’s most populated regions. The calculation tells us how widely nature is offering the view. Conditions on the ground, and whether people remember to look up, will decide how many accept it.
b84b561bac4cfbcb0c86dfbb.summary: On April 13, 2029, the asteroid Apophis will safely pass about 32,000 kilometres above Earth, coming closer than geostationary satellites. New calculations indicate that up to 7.6 billion people, or roughly 90% of humanity, live within regions where the asteroid could theoretically be seen with the naked eye. However, actual visibility will depend on local weather, light pollution, terrain, and whether individuals choose to look up during the seven-hour viewing window.
key_points: Asteroid Apophis will make a close, safe flyby of Earth on April 13, 2029, passing approximately 32,000 kilometres above the surface.
NASA and ESA have confirmed that Apophis poses no impact risk to Earth for at least the next century.
Visibility maps presented in June 2026 estimate that 7.6 billion people live within the cumulative viewing footprint, though they will not all see it at the exact same time.
During its closest approach, Apophis will appear to the naked eye as a modest, steadily moving star rather than a burning meteor.
The 90% potential audience figure represents access in principle and is subject to local weather, urban light pollution, and other viewing obstructions.

4956d23030a48da0bd172e2b.title: Rising number of people seeking ADHD diagnosis without treatment, say experts
4956d23030a48da0bd172e2b.author: Rachel Hall
4956d23030a48da0bd172e2b.content:
People are increasingly seeking to an obtain an ADHD diagnosis without pursuing treatment, according to experts who have called for more research to understand why.
Some people now regard ADHD as “an identity, rather than a disorder”, with the result that many obtain assessments from poor quality private providers, which lead them to “believe they have a condition needing treatment”, said the psychiatrist Dr Marios Adamou, the founder of the UK Adult ADHD Network.
This has resulted in a growth in complaints against NHS doctors when they are forced to reject low quality assessments, he added.
Adamou had seen recent figures showing that 50% of child patients did not pursue treatment after diagnosis, and observed a similar trend among adult patients in his clinic.
Some patients seek low, non-therapeutic doses of medication instead. “A lot of people would benefit from having amphetamines. You feel better, you can focus better, you can do more. But there hasn’t been a debate that this country should be cognitively augmented to increase productivity with stimulants,” he said.
“Why do people feel they can identify with these conditions? They are manifestations of a societal problem.”
Adamou was speaking ahead of a new Channel 4 documentary airing on 18 August titled The Great ADHD Myth?. It is presented by the NHS psychiatrist Dr Max Pemberton, who concludes that ADHD is a “social construct” rather than a medical condition, and that schools should adapt to better support a wider range of children rather than medicating them into fitting into a restrictive norm.
![Mother Shauna stands behind son Mason, her hands on his shoulders.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/428419d49712225c1ab892af5ae1ca0bb0a40f06/0_0_3354_4000/master/3354.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Adamou said that ADHD was both a social construct and a brain disorder. Brain differences are well established through research, and the diagnostic criteria has undergone “a lot of scientific scrutiny and validation”, he said, but added that in recent years “the ADHD concept has been expanded so much, it’s risking becoming meaningless … it’s socially constructed now, it’s something different than what it actually is.”
He said this phenomenon was fuelled by “challenges with the quality and the regulation of the [ADHD services] market”.
“Most of the assessment in the UK is now provided by the private sector,” he said. “I don’t think there’s any other medical condition where the private sector provides as much care … When you have private providers providing the majority of care in a market system with a diagnosis that is commoditised, and attracts stimulants, you may have issues.”
Despite this, he stressed that there was thought to be underdiagnosis of ADHD. Poor quality diagnoses have created “a double stigma” for many people with the condition. “Not only do you have stigma because you have ADHD, but also there’s stigma about whether you have real ADHD,” he said.
Prof Dinesh Bhugra, the former head of the Royal College of Psychiatrists who features in the documentary, agreed that “there has certainly been a splurge of diagnosis, and we don’t know why that is”.
He said: “The question is why now, and why this? What is it providing? My fear is we medicalise normal human responses because it gives us the power as clinicians and it gives people the label which allows them to either feel they’ve got certain privileges or it gives them certain cachet in society.”
In the documentary, he shares his concerns about the growing role of profiteering private companies supplying services that the NHS is under too much strain to provide. ADHD assessment was “an easy way to make money” for private companies, he said, adding: “Their responsibility is to the shareholders, not the general public.”
Bhugra feared that the UK’s current approach was an American import, where the DSM [Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders]’s checklist-style approach to assessment reflected the demands of insurance companies, and a culture of “health is a commodity and you can buy it and sell it”.
He agreed with the documentary’s message that services should be reformed to take a more holistic approach, bringing together the social, biological and psychological facts of ADHD rather than emphasising medical intervention.
Jessica Lister, a clinical director and consultant nurse at the private provider Care ADHD, feared that the documentary’s message could be harmful. “Dismissing ADHD as a social construct doesn’t just trivialise an established clinical condition – it perpetuates the inequalities faced by people with ADHD across education, health, employment and the justice system,” she said.
“The question here isn’t whether ADHD is a real medical problem – it’s whether systems respond early enough, consistently enough and fairly enough to prevent avoidable harm … The real problems are long waits, inequitable access, inconsistent quality and too little joined-up support across health, education, care and employment.”
Mark Pattison, the chief executive of Care ADHD, said that it was important to differentiate between private providers, adding that his organisation’s clinical governance was as strong as the NHS ADHD and mental health services he had run for 15 years. “Profit should never come before clinical quality. But efficiency isn’t the enemy of it either,” he said.
He added: “Standards need to apply to everyone, not just us. Some NHS trusts have children waiting two, five, even 10 years for an assessment. That’s not safe care, whoever provides it. Some private providers fall short too.”
The Great ADHD Myth? is available to watch and stream on Channel 4 at 8pm, Tuesday 18 August.
4956d23030a48da0bd172e2b.summary: Experts report a rising number of individuals seeking ADHD diagnoses without pursuing treatment, often viewing the condition as an identity rather than a disorder. This trend is linked by some to poor-quality private providers, a commoditised diagnostic market, and the medicalisation of normal human responses. While critics argue ADHD is becoming a meaningless social construct, other clinical professionals warn that dismissing the condition trivializes a real medical issue and worsens existing inequalities.
key_points: Experts have observed a growing trend of adults and children obtaining ADHD diagnoses without following through with treatment.
Concerns have been raised regarding poor-quality private providers and a commoditised market system that issues low-quality assessments.
A forthcoming Channel 4 documentary features psychiatrists debating whether ADHD is a medical condition or a social construct.
Some clinicians fear that normal human responses are being medicalized, creating a double stigma for individuals with genuine ADHD.
Representatives from private providers caution that dismissing ADHD as a social construct perpetuates inequalities and ignores systemic failings like long NHS wait times.

197eabeddafdb4cdf2937da3.title: Body found in Wylam river search for missing soldier Liam Potts
197eabeddafdb4cdf2937da3.author: Caroline Briggs
197eabeddafdb4cdf2937da3.content:
![Search and rescue team of four in the River Tyne in Wylam. Two are wearing red helmets, one has a yellow helmet and the fourth is in white. They are wearing red and yellow waterproof clothing and red lifesaver jackets. Each has a pole with which they appear to prodding into the water, which is a murky green. Beyond them and in the foreground are trees, shrubs and other vegetation.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/976/cpsprodpb/ce9d/live/f5fd15f0-9b27-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Search and rescue workers have been scouring the river
- Published
Police searching for a soldier who went missing after spending the night with friends say they have found a body.
Liam Potts, 22, who served with the Coldstream Guards, was last seen heading towards Wylam in Northumberland from Wylam Bridge at about 00:20 BST on Saturday.

747e1261bdbe2d1351258388.title: Earthquake rocks Spain's historic Granada, injuring three
747e1261bdbe2d1351258388.author: Jaroslav Lukiv
747e1261bdbe2d1351258388.content:
Watch: Terrified pets and crushed cars as earthquake shakes Granada
- Published
At least three people have been lightly injured and a number of buildings damaged after an earthquake rocked southern Spain.
The epicentre of the magnitude 4.8 tremor on Tuesday morning was about 10km (six miles) south of the historic city of Granada, the country's National Geographic Institute (IGN) said.
Many local residents were seen rushing out of their homes into the streets, fearing strong aftershocks. A number of vehicles were damaged by falling debris. Some museums, administrative buildings and sports centres have been forced to close.
The IGN said it was the latest in a series of very shallow tremors in the area that started last Friday and were widely felt.
![A policeman stands at a cordoned off street near damaged vehicles following an earthquake in Granada, southern Spain. Photo: 18 August 2026](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/831b/live/65230d80-9b24-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
A number of vehicles were damaged by falling debris in Tuesday's earthquake
The tremor struck at 10:37 local time (08:37 GMT) near the town of AlhendÃn, the IGN said. It was recorded at the depth of under 10km.
Alfonso Malpica said he felt his ground floor flat in Granada shaking, telling El PaÃs newspaper that the quake was "stronger than the ones that happen from time to time, the ones we're used to".
"Everything came crashing down. It was terrifying," Cristina Ruiz Lopez, a lab worker who was at a supermarket in Granada, was quoted as saying by the AFP news agency.
Granada's famous Alhambra palace - a Unesco World Heritage Site of medieval Islamic architecture - "will remain closed this afternoon", the site administrators said.
The palace is visited every year by millions of tourists from around the world.
Meanwhile, Granada's metro network said it was reducing the speed of its trains to 30km/h (19mph) for "safety reasons" and warned that this may cause delays.
747e1261bdbe2d1351258388.summary: An earthquake with a magnitude of 4.8 struck southern Spain near Granada, resulting in three light injuries and building damage. Residents fled to the streets as falling debris damaged vehicles and forced the closure of museums, administrative buildings, and sports centres, including the famous Alhambra palace. The tremor was part of a series of shallow earthquakes that began the previous Friday in the area.
key_points: A 4.8 magnitude earthquake hit southern Spain near Granada on Tuesday morning.
At least three people sustained light injuries and several vehicles were damaged by falling debris.
The historic Alhambra palace and other public buildings were temporarily closed.
The tremor was the latest in a series of shallow earthquakes in the region that began on Friday.

d01917ce356b62b98d8daf5f.title: Meet the modern-day Medicis: inside the glamorous world of London's young patrons
d01917ce356b62b98d8daf5f.author: Isolde Walters
d01917ce356b62b98d8daf5f.content:
After dark in London’s haute cultural institutions, a new social scene is emerging. Insiders, on any given evening, will find a coterie of bright young things swirling martinis beneath the startled gaze of Whistlejacket in the National Gallery, or grazing on canapés after hours among the marble statues in the Cast Courts at the V&A Museum. Forget benefactors in twinsets and pearls, these modern-day Medicis are young and well-connected, with deep pockets and a penchant for parties, couture and access.
Welcome to the world of the young patrons: a fresh generation of philanthropists, armed with Amexes and ambition. They are, of course, being welcomed famously. The V&A, Tate, National Gallery, Serpentine and Wallace Collection have all created young patrons’ schemes. In return for an annual fee of around £1,200 and with the hope that one or two of these budding Peggy Guggenheims may in time become big-deal donors (the type with their name on the wing) there are prodigious perks. Think behind-the-scenes tours, invitations to glitzy opening nights, summer parties, studio visits, mystery dinners, rooftop drinks and lavish trips to Paris, Turin and private Venetian palazzos. For the young, cultured rich, it is the ultimate status symbol.
The Marchioness of Bute has announced she is closing her eponymous fashion label, Serena Bute London. The clothes – loved by Poppy Delevingne, Rita Ora and so many more – never looked more glamorous than when they were modelled by Serena and her daughter, Lady Lola, at the family seat of Mount Stuart, the staggering four-storey Victorian Gothic fantasy on the Hebridean Isle of Bute
![article image](https://media.tatler.com/photos/6141e125797f8a06f4b68170/master/w_775%2Cc_limit/tatler-bute-6.jpg)
The schemes fly under the radar with very little advertisement, so although they are technically open to anyone who will pony up the yearly fee, in practise they operate like private members’ clubs, with patrons coming via word-of-mouth and personal recommendation. And, like any hot scene, it’s becoming tribal.
You’ll find the financiers and lawyers populating the National Gallery’s Young Ambassadors programme, where there’s an air of seriousness and perhaps – according to one art-world insider – fustiness. The V&A’s set is rather more feminine, sequinned and, many say, fun, with the lure of a sought-after invitation to the museum’s summer party a key draw. The Tate clique is very south London, with a taste for social causes and conceptual fashion; while the World Monuments Fund crowd is unabashedly international. Meanwhile you’ll find fashionistas flocking to the Serpentine’s Future Contemporaries young patrons programme.
Heading to Oxford? Whether you're a religious rower, a union hack, or a Right Hon, as results day rolls around, here's a totally objective, comprehensive guide to the college you're about to call home
But there’s no competition when it comes to which scheme reigns supreme on the London social scene. ‘The number one has to be the V&A’ says Žanete Bukarte, a Latvian lawyer and hobby sculptor, who is a young patron of four different institutions, including the museum in South Kensington. ‘The V&A curated a very vibrant crowd, helped by the location of the museum and word-of-mouth.’ Euthymia Procopé, the social butterfly hired to scatter a little society dust over the V&A’s young patrons’ programme, is in full agreement. ‘It is the jewel in the crown,’ she declares.
Established in 2016, and inspired by similar schemes at MoMA and the Frick in New York, the V&A Young Patron’s Circle began with the long-term goal of engaging young people in the hope that they would become absolute devotees of the museum and ideally, budding philanthropists. With a wide age range of 20 to 40, the scheme attracted international students as well as established lawyers and hedgefunders. And with jewellery designer Cora Sheibani – daughter of Bruno Bischofberger, the prominent Swiss art dealer known for his close associations with Jean-Michel Basquiat and Andy Warhol – as a founding co-chair, the programme wielded social power from the outset.
But Procopé, the scheme’s senior manager from 2021 to 2023, knew she could turn it up a notch, and she set about making the Young Patrons’ Circle a hotbed of socialites, redesigning its brochures and bringing in Flora Vesterberg as her co-chair.
The great and the gilded flocked to South Somerset when billionaire Koos Bekker built The Newt hotel. Some locals, however, feared it brought an end to their countryside way of life. Isolde Walters investigated the feud igniting the Green and Pleasant Land.
![Image may contain: Grass, Nature, Outdoors, Park, Plant, Land, Vegetation, Tree, Woodland, Scenery, Water, and Architecture](https://media.tatler.com/photos/6a7b022d9a0d012454c1c599/master/w_775%2Cc_limit/The%2520Newt%2520Estate.%2520The%2520Newt%2520In%2520Somerset.%2520Credit%2520The%2520Newt%2520In%2520Somerset.jpg)
‘I wanted to make it really sociable, and Flora was great,’ she says. ‘She would invite Amelia Windsor and Princess Beatrice to the Young Patrons’ annual party.’ Freddie and Sophie Windsor attended two years on the trot, rubbing shoulders with Tatler’s social editor Davina Chelsea. Society’s favourite royal DJ, Cassius Taylor, took over the decks in front of the museum’s medieval and Renaissance sculptures in 2023, while this year the patrons decamped to the V&A’s new east London outpost, where Tristram Hunt held court with Lord Ogilvy.
The strategy worked, and during Procopé and Vesterberg’s tenure, Viscountess Newport, Petrina Hesketh, the Countess of Belfast and Pamela Weinstock-Perry all became Young Patrons. But to keep the It girls happy, the perks had to match the parties. ‘The USP was that you’d get this incredible access to the museum out of hours… first-thing-in-the-morning visits and curator-led tours,’ says Procopé. There were trips abroad to tighten those all-important social bonds – such as the 2022 trip to Florence, which took in the Donatello exhibition at Palazzo Strozzi and a tour of Gucci’s private design archives, before finishing up with a drinks party at the former home of John Pope-Hennessy, one of the previous directors of the museum.
Romance occasionally flourishes between young patrons. ‘People do use it as a dating opportunity,’ Procopé says. ‘I know of several examples where romance has absolutely struck. You’d notice on day trips – people talking a lot and holding hands.’
But for socialites in search of The One, the V&A’s unfavourable female-to-male ratio is hardly ideal. According to one insider, the only patron’s programme to join if on the hunt for love is the National Gallery’s Young Ambassadors, as it’s where the men, with reassuringly high-flying careers in law, finance and tech, are. Former Tatler cover star Sabine Getty teamed up with Harriet Roseberry as co-chairs to launch the £1,200-a-year membership in 2021. A year later, financier Jacques-Louis de la Beraudiere and art tech CEO Sam Glatman were among the eligibles on board.
Bukarte, who is also a Young Ambassador (the scheme’s name is a nod to the gallery’s famous Holbein painting), describes the hallowed institution’s youthful coterie as a ‘very elegant, very poised crowd, full of people who are deeply knowledgeable about the art world already, or hold very important roles in the finance or legal worlds. Very adult, quite serious.’ That comes with its challenges. One Young Ambassador, who shall remain nameless, describes the group as ‘academic’, with room for improvement when it comes to parties. ‘It’s such a huge space to fill – you have to have so many people there for it to feel like a vibe… There was a party for the Sainsbury Wing, and there were hundreds and hundreds of people there; it didn’t really feel as friendly and intimate as the V&A parties.’
The Junior Board of the World Monuments Fund has no such difficulty with its parties – the last one was a lavish affair at Horace Walpole’s neo-Gothic Strawberry Hill mansion. Data scientist Ege Gürmeriçliler, who serves as a co-chair, was the star attraction. ‘He’s gorgeous and extraordinarily rich, and the girls were all over him like bees on honey,’ one attendee recalls. ‘He spends all day working on AI models in his flat in west London, but he pours his passion into the World Monuments Fund.’
Buried in the Surrey Hills, Beaverbrook once played host to an earlier generation of Hollywood greats. This week, it was the turn of tinseltown’s reigning king and queen: Tom Holland and Zendaya, who celebrated their marriage by booking out the entire estate. But there’s so much beyond the caviar-infused omakase and chequerboard swimming pool, reveals Delilah Khomo
![article image](https://media.tatler.com/photos/618910e137fe9b2985bd366f/master/w_775%2Cc_limit/Beaverbrookspa0892%2520%2520.jpeg)
The contrast between a serious (and often lucrative) career and the opportunity to lose oneself in art in the evenings is key for young patrons. ‘The finance tribe love the contrast between crunching numbers and then coming to something arty as a change of scene,’ says Procopé. There is also the ageless flex of art patronage – just as the Medicis realised the cultural capital to be gained from supporting Michelangelo and da Vinci, today’s young patrons are using the prestige in a uniquely 21st-century manner. ‘People put it in their LinkedIn profiles and on their Instagram bios,’ Procopé says. ‘People like the cachet of being able to say, “I am a patron, I am a supporter of this art institution” – and it does carry social clout.’
Then there’s the access. For a relatively affordable annual membership fee, society’s doors are thrown open to the young patron. You may find yourself at a World Monuments Fund event, mixing with the youngest generation of the Niarchos family or travelling with the heiress to the Bacardi fortune. ‘It’s a brilliant way of meeting people,’ Bukarte enthuses. ‘You get exposed to people a regular person would not. Most of these people are not that regular: they are very well-connected, or come from prominent families.’
Unsurprisingly, the Tate's Young Patrons are more democratic – they get a say on how funds they raise are spent by the museum – and they are more interested in social causes. While the young art aficionados have flown on Tate trips before, now a sustainability drive means only destinations accessible by Eurostar are on the cards. Still, they managed to net Princess Eugenie as an ambassador and arranged parties in the Tank Rooms at Tate Modern, rooftop soirées, and back-to-school drinks at the Arts Club, Ladbroke Hall and Annabel’s.
Gulru Arvas, an architect based in west London but originally from Istanbul, who served as a co-chair, describes the tribe as a diverse mix of professions. ‘At a young patrons’ dinner, I would chat with an artist, then someone who works in finance, a mathematician, someone in film and another patron in oil and gas.’ The dress code? ‘edgy, a lot of Margiela, that kind of thing.’
Arvas – known as Gu – has just become a member of the Serpentine Galleries’ young patrons’ scheme, Future Contemporaries, lured by the VIP breakfast at Zaha Hadid-designed restaurant The Magazine –‘it’s a really fun way to kick of Frieze Week’ – and the gallery’s Mystery Nights, where young patrons are split up into small groups, and given a time and a place to meet and dine in the fabulous homes of select art collectors. The difference between the Tate crowd and the Serpentine crowd? ‘They dress up a little more.’ Think all-black and very fashion.
Many young patrons can’t resist supporting multiple institutions, which can make their social calendar even more hectic, particularly during summer party week or when Frieze is on.‘There is a tribe that belongs to all of these groups and circulates around, going to several events per evening, running from the Tate to the Serpentine,’ Bukarte says. ‘That forms a community element in its own right, because if you attend these gatherings for a sufficient period of time, you already know who the other people are who go to these institutions as well. Often you share a black cab and run around London with these people. You end up going to dinner together or going to 5 Hertford Street afterwards, as many of these events take place on a Thursday night.’
With rumours that the British Museum and National Portrait Gallery are soon to launch their own young patrons’ programmes, and with the Wallace Collection’s Young Benefactors scheme attracting new members, the hot young philanthropists striding through the capital’s cultural scene are set to multiply.
The only question left to ask is: what tribe of young patrons do you belong to? The art might be priceless, but the guest list is the real masterpiece.
This feature was originally published in the January 2026 issue of Tatler and remains unedited.

For an annual fee of around £1,200, members gain access to exclusive perks such as after-hours tours, international trips, and high-profile social events. These programs function similarly to private members' clubs, offering participants a mix of networking, romance, and cultural prestige.

Perks include private curator-led tours, exclusive parties, and international trips to locations like Florence and Venice.
Different museums attract distinct social tribes, ranging from the V&A's glamorous society crowd to the National Gallery's finance-heavy Young Ambassadors.
Membership provides high-status networking opportunities, social clout, and access to well-connected peers and prominent families.

![Image may contain: Grass, Nature, Outdoors, Park, Plant, Land, Vegetation, Tree, Woodland, Scenery, Water, and Architecture](https://media.tatler.com/photos/6a7b022d9a0d012454c1c599/master/w_775%2Cc_limit/The%2520Newt%2520Estate.%2520The%2520Newt%2520In%2520Somerset.%2520Credit%2520The%2520Newt%2520In%2520Somerset.jpg)
‘I wanted to make it really sociable, and Flora was great,’ she says. ‘She would invite Amelia Windsor and Princess Beatrice to the Young Patrons’ annual party.’ Freddie and Sophie Windsor attended two years on the trot, rubbing shoulders with Tatler’s social editor Davina Chelsea. Society’s favourite royal DJ, Cassius Taylor, took over the decks in front of the museum’s medieval and Renaissance sculptures in 2023, while this year the patrons decamped to the V&A’s new east London outpost, where Tristram Hunt held court with Lord Ogilvy.
The strategy worked, and during Procopé and Vesterberg’s tenure, Viscountess Newport, Petrina Hesketh, the Countess of Belfast and Pamela Weinstock-Perry all became Young Patrons. But to keep the It girls happy, the perks had to match the parties. ‘The USP was that you’d get this incredible access to the museum out of hours… first-thing-in-the-morning visits and curator-led tours,’ says Procopé. There were trips abroad to tighten those all-important social bonds – such as the 2022 trip to Florence, which took in the Donatello exhibition at Palazzo Strozzi and a tour of Gucci’s private design archives, before finishing up with a drinks party at the former home of John Pope-Hennessy, one of the previous directors of the museum.
Romance occasionally flourishes between young patrons. ‘People do use it as a dating opportunity,’ Procopé says. ‘I know of several examples where romance has absolutely struck. You’d notice on day trips – people talking a lot and holding hands.’
But for socialites in search of The One, the V&A’s unfavourable female-to-male ratio is hardly ideal. According to one insider, the only patron’s programme to join if on the hunt for love is the National Gallery’s Young Ambassadors, as it’s where the men, with reassuringly high-flying careers in law, finance and tech, are. Former Tatler cover star Sabine Getty teamed up with Harriet Roseberry as co-chairs to launch the £1,200-a-year membership in 2021. A year later, financier Jacques-Louis de la Beraudiere and art tech CEO Sam Glatman were among the eligibles on board.
Bukarte, who is also a Young Ambassador (the scheme’s name is a nod to the gallery’s famous Holbein painting), describes the hallowed institution’s youthful coterie as a ‘very elegant, very poised crowd, full of people who are deeply knowledgeable about the art world already, or hold very important roles in the finance or legal worlds. Very adult, quite serious.’ That comes with its challenges. One Young Ambassador, who shall remain nameless, describes the group as ‘academic’, with room for improvement when it comes to parties. ‘It’s such a huge space to fill – you have to have so many people there for it to feel like a vibe… There was a party for the Sainsbury Wing, and there were hundreds and hundreds of people there; it didn’t really feel as friendly and intimate as the V&A parties.’
The Junior Board of the World Monuments Fund has no such difficulty with its parties – the last one was a lavish affair at Horace Walpole’s neo-Gothic Strawberry Hill mansion. Data scientist Ege Gürmeriçliler, who serves as a co-chair, was the star attraction. ‘He’s gorgeous and extraordinarily rich, and the girls were all over him like bees on honey,’ one attendee recalls. ‘He spends all day working on AI models in his flat in west London, but he pours his passion into the World Monuments Fund.’
Buried in the Surrey Hills, Beaverbrook once played host to an earlier generation of Hollywood greats. This week, it was the turn of tinseltown’s reigning king and queen: Tom Holland and Zendaya, who celebrated their marriage by booking out the entire estate. But there’s so much beyond the caviar-infused omakase and chequerboard swimming pool, reveals Delilah Khomo
![article image](https://media.tatler.com/photos/618910e137fe9b2985bd366f/master/w_775%2Cc_limit/Beaverbrookspa0892%2520%2520.jpeg)
The contrast between a serious (and often lucrative) career and the opportunity to lose oneself in art in the evenings is key for young patrons. ‘The finance tribe love the contrast between crunching numbers and then coming to something arty as a change of scene,’ says Procopé. There is also the ageless flex of art patronage – just as the Medicis realised the cultural capital to be gained from supporting Michelangelo and da Vinci, today’s young patrons are using the prestige in a uniquely 21st-century manner. ‘People put it in their LinkedIn profiles and on their Instagram bios,’ Procopé says. ‘People like the cachet of being able to say, “I am a patron, I am a supporter of this art institution” – and it does carry social clout.’
Then there’s the access. For a relatively affordable annual membership fee, society’s doors are thrown open to the young patron. You may find yourself at a World Monuments Fund event, mixing with the youngest generation of the Niarchos family or travelling with the heiress to the Bacardi fortune. ‘It’s a brilliant way of meeting people,’ Bukarte enthuses. ‘You get exposed to people a regular person would not. Most of these people are not that regular: they are very well-connected, or come from prominent families.’
Unsurprisingly, the Tate's Young Patrons are more democratic – they get a say on how funds they raise are spent by the museum – and they are more interested in social causes. While the young art aficionados have flown on Tate trips before, now a sustainability drive means only destinations accessible by Eurostar are on the cards. Still, they managed to net Princess Eugenie as an ambassador and arranged parties in the Tank Rooms at Tate Modern, rooftop soirées, and back-to-school drinks at the Arts Club, Ladbroke Hall and Annabel’s.
Gulru Arvas, an architect based in west London but originally from Istanbul, who served as a co-chair, describes the tribe as a diverse mix of professions. ‘At a young patrons’ dinner, I would chat with an artist, then someone who works in finance, a mathematician, someone in film and another patron in oil and gas.’ The dress code? ‘edgy, a lot of Margiela, that kind of thing.’
Arvas – known as Gu – has just become a member of the Serpentine Galleries’ young patrons’ scheme, Future Contemporaries, lured by the VIP breakfast at Zaha Hadid-designed restaurant The Magazine –‘it’s a really fun way to kick of Frieze Week’ – and the gallery’s Mystery Nights, where young patrons are split up into small groups, and given a time and a place to meet and dine in the fabulous homes of select art collectors. The difference between the Tate crowd and the Serpentine crowd? ‘They dress up a little more.’ Think all-black and very fashion.
Many young patrons can’t resist supporting multiple institutions, which can make their social calendar even more hectic, particularly during summer party week or when Frieze is on.‘There is a tribe that belongs to all of these groups and circulates around, going to several events per evening, running from the Tate to the Serpentine,’ Bukarte says. ‘That forms a community element in its own right, because if you attend these gatherings for a sufficient period of time, you already know who the other people are who go to these institutions as well. Often you share a black cab and run around London with these people. You end up going to dinner together or going to 5 Hertford Street afterwards, as many of these events take place on a Thursday night.’
With rumours that the British Museum and National Portrait Gallery are soon to launch their own young patrons’ programmes, and with the Wallace Collection’s Young Benefactors scheme attracting new members, the hot young philanthropists striding through the capital’s cultural scene are set to multiply.
The only question left to ask is: what tribe of young patrons do you belong to? The art might be priceless, but the guest list is the real masterpiece.
This feature was originally published in the January 2026 issue of Tatler and remains unedited.

8428848c7f018223f5cd1a92.summary: London's major cultural institutions, including the V&A, Tate, and National Gallery, have established young patrons' schemes targeting affluent individuals aged 20 to 40. For an annual fee of around £1,200, members gain access to exclusive perks such as after-hours tours, international trips, and high-profile social events. These programs function similarly to private members' clubs, offering participants a mix of networking, romance, and cultural prestige.
key_points: Institutions like the V&A, Tate, National Gallery, Serpentine, and World Monuments Fund offer young patron memberships for roughly £1,200 a year.
Perks include private curator-led tours, exclusive parties, and international trips to locations like Florence and Venice.
Different museums attract distinct social tribes, ranging from the V&A's glamorous society crowd to the National Gallery's finance-heavy Young Ambassadors.
Membership provides high-status networking opportunities, social clout, and access to well-connected peers and prominent families.

f041dd01bc884e8ccc01fac6.title: Global bond markets ‘on fire’ as borrowing costs soar
f041dd01bc884e8ccc01fac6.author: Szu Ping Chan
f041dd01bc884e8ccc01fac6.content:
![John Healey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/18/TELEMMGLPICT000495951398_17870683561230_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq3XmyF3YIL3K1caQxZsZv2eil7a1KV2STY3xRqqFt_No.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![John Healey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/18/TELEMMGLPICT000495951398_17870683561230_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq3XmyF3YIL3K1caQxZsZv2eil7a1KV2STY3xRqqFt_No.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Borrowing costs have surged to the levels seen in the run up to the financial crisis on fears that governments are losing control of debt.
An increasingly toxic cocktail of the Iran conflict, the AI industry’s unprecedented surge in borrowing and inflation fears sent the yield on 30-year US Treasuries to a two-decade high of 5.33pc on Tuesday. Yields on benchmark 10-year US debt also rose as high as 4.74pc.
In Britain, the Debt Management Office sold government bonds carrying the highest interest rate since 2007. Some £4bn in gilts were issued with a yield of 5.155pc, the highest rate since just before Northern Rock collapsed.
Rising debt costs are posing a headache for John Healey, the Chancellor, who is preparing to unveil his maiden Budget on Oct 28.
The problem is not confined to Britain and the US. Borrowing costs in Japan are at a 30-year high and France’s 10-year bond yield on Tuesday hit its highest level since 2009.
Robin Brooks, at the Brookings Institution, said global bond markets were “on fire” as investors lose faith in the ability of governments to get debt down.
“When you have a lot of debt and run unsustainably large budget deficits, you’re extremely vulnerable to any old shock that comes along,” he said. “It’s not about the shock, but – instead – the mess we are making of fiscal policy on a global scale.”
The former economist at the International Monetary Fund warned that countries with “lots of debt and political dysfunction” such as the UK, France and Japan were “being hit harder than others”.
By contrast, more prudent countries such as Switzerland and Germany have been more insulated, though the borrowing costs of both increased on Tuesday.
Britain’s debt pile is already close to 100pc of GDP, while France and Japan have even higher debt shares.
Mr Brooks said investors were demanding a higher premium for long-term borrowing amid growing uncertainty regarding the political and economic outlook for debt-laden countries.
“Initial conditions turn out to be massively important,” he said. “The benefits of responsible fiscal policy ... have never been more apparent.”
While investor demand for British debt remains robust, with more than three buyers bidding for every bond on offer, economists said rising borrowing costs served as a warning to Andy Burnham.
The Prime Minister and Mr Healey are seeking to borrow more by exploiting flexibility in the fiscal rules introduced by Rachel Reeves, the previous chancellor.
The new Chancellor is exploring ways to boost investment at a time when rising prices and borrowing costs, driven by conflict in the Middle East, have already eaten into half of Mr Healey’s £24bn buffer to balance the books.
‘A warning sign’ to Healey
Exploiting flexibilities in the fiscal rules risks pushing up borrowing costs even further and adding yet more pressure to the public finances.
Simon French, the chief UK economist at Panmure Liberum, said: “This is a warning to the Chancellor on the risks of using the flexibilities in the fiscal rules to increase borrowing. It can be done, but at a cost, and quite a punishing one for future taxpayers.”
Economists warn that inflation could come close to 4pc by the end of this year, from less than 3pc today. This will add to pressure on the public finances and push up the cost of owning a home.
The Bank of England has signalled that interest rates will have to stay higher for longer to keep a lid on inflation, prompting mortgage lenders to push up the cost of consumer borrowing.
US mortgage rates have also climbed to their highest rates in more than a year, with home loans closely linked to long-term borrowing costs.
Economists are predicting that the US national debt could surpass $40tn (£30tn) this week after a Supreme Court ruling on Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs blew a hole in his budget plans.
Official forecasts show that the US’s debt pile is on course to hit $39.4tn this fiscal year ending in September. However, the treasury admitted this week that total debt has already hit $39.9tn.
The White House has also warned that countries such as China are increasingly sending their exports through other countries to avoid US tariffs, costing the Trump administration up to $26bn a year.

Countries with high debt and political dysfunction, such as the UK, US, France, and Japan, are facing the steepest yield increases and mounting fiscal pressures. Economists warn that these rising costs and potential increases in borrowing serve as a stark warning to governments regarding unsustainable budget deficits.

Global borrowing costs are surging due to a combination of the Iran conflict, high AI industry borrowing, and inflation fears.
Countries with high debt shares and political dysfunction, including the UK, France, and Japan, are being hit harder than more prudent nations like Switzerland and Germany.
UK Chancellor John Healey faces a growing budget headache as rising prices and borrowing costs eat into his financial buffer ahead of the October Budget.
Economists warn that exploiting fiscal flexibilities to increase borrowing risks pushing up debt costs further and penalizing future taxpayers.

51421d7ce8120064fc9280ab.title: Campaigner Claire Lomas died in crash while filming Apple series, inquest told
51421d7ce8120064fc9280ab.author: Dan Hunt
51421d7ce8120064fc9280ab.content:
![An image of Claire Lomas with a Great North Run sign behind her](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/575e/live/ecab1300-989c-11f0-8e62-81f400027fcb.jpg)
Claire Lomas raised nearly Â£1m for charity, and was the first person to complete a marathon in a "bionic" suit
- Published
A campaigner who raised nearly Â£1m for charity during her life was "excited" about taking part in a microlighting filming project for an Apple headset before she died, an inquest has heard.
Claire Lomas began fundraising after a 2007 horse riding accident left her paralysed, with her efforts including completing the 2012 London Marathon in a "bionic" suit.
Her inquest was told Lomas was flying an adapted microlight in Jordan on 15 July 2024 when it veered off a road after landing and crashed into a large rock.
The court heard she was then taken to the King Hussein Medical Centre, where Lomas's condition improved before she had a "sudden deterioration" and died on 22 August.
'Very enthusiastic and keen'
Louise Pinder, senior coroner for Rutland and North Leicestershire, said Lomas's provisional cause of death was multiple severe traumatic injuries.
The inquest, which is being held at County Hall, heard Lomas - from Eye Kettleby, near Melton Mowbray in Leicestershire - was in Jordan to take part in an Apple-commissioned series called Adventure, which involved filming athletes in "spectacular" locations.
Lina Zilinskaite, senior producer for Atlantic Productions - the company commissioned to film the series - said the firm reached out to Lomas about taking part in a microlighting project.
Zilinskaite told the inquest Lomas was "really delighted" about the opportunity and the company was "reassured" that she had some previous experience with media.
"She was very enthusiastic and keen and excited about the opportunity," Zilinskaite said.
The court heard she had obtained a licence to fly a microlight - a type of small aircraft - a few years before and had limited experience of about 150 hours.
Zilinskaite said the company contacted Ben Ashman, from Flylight Airsports, about her limitations, which informed them she was a "talented pilot" but needed assistance getting in and out of the microlight.
![Claire Lomas holds a flaming torch over a steel cauldron](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/678/cpsprodpb/8c3d/live/47a7c900-80bc-11ef-9552-f58ba4473009.png)
Lomas lit a cauldron as part of the torch relay for the Paralympic Games in 2012
The inquest heard a camera was mounted to the microlight, and tests were carried out with Ashman and Lomas flying the microlight with the camera.
Zilinskaite told the court Lomas was "very happy" and it seemed she had "no concerns".
The court was told Lomas flew to Jordan on 10 July 2024 - and the challenge was initially earmarked to take place on 14 July, however, it did not take place as it was "too windy".
On 15 July, the inquest heard Zilinskaite and Ashman were at the filming location at about 04:00, when they had a conversation about the wind being "good".
However, she added Ashman was "concerned" about a Facebook post from Lomas the night before - and they decided to have a conversation with her at the hotel about whether she wanted to go ahead with the challenge.
Zilinskaite said Lomas was "enthusiastic" and was "absolutely sure she wanted to fly".
The inquest heard the flight took about 15 minutes - with Ashman landing and clearing the runway before Lomas made her approach.
Zilinskaite said she raised her phone to record Lomas's landing, however she did not press record as Lomas's approach "wasn't quite straight on".
She added she did not see the crash as her view was blocked - but said Lomas was taken by ambulance to Petra, then taken by air ambulance to Amman.
Lomas was "excited" to come home with her family after spending weeks in hospital but then contracted an infection and deteriorated, the inquest heard.
The coroner said Lomas's relatives were concerned about the care she received at the hospital in Jordan, but added it was not within her jurisdiction to investigate that formally.
![Claire Lomas, on crutches and wearing a robotic suit to brace her lower body, crosses the finish line for the Great North Run](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/914/cpsprodpb/8ed5/live/3f84c010-80c2-11ef-ab28-17c883eb03dd.png)
Before her death, Lomas raised Â£952,000 for charity
Giving evidence to the inquest, Ashman - a microlight designer and manufacturer at Flylight Airsports - said Lomas bought her own aircraft in 2022 or 2023, which the company adapted so there were no controls at her feet.
He said he was concerned Lomas was stressed before the flight because she posted on Facebook about putting her "brave pants" on, which was "unusual" for her.
He said he spoke to her, adding: "She said 'let's do it'. I didn't want to turn around and say 'you shouldn't do it'. I didn't want to take away her confidence."
Ashman, who was in Jordan at the time, said Lomas's microlight descended at 20 degrees away from the centre of the runway, and she appeared to try to stop her landing effort.
The inquest heard there were no issues with the weather, no mechanical issues, and the 180-degree camera did not affect the flight of the aircraft.
'Bionic woman'
Lomas was told she would never walk again after she was thrown from her horse at the Osberton Horse Trials in Nottinghamshire in 2007, but a suit with mechanical legs, called ReWalk, helped her to take her first steps again at a rehabilitation centre in East Yorkshire five years later.
The suit used braces to support the legs, motors to help rotate joints, weight and motion sensors and a battery pack.
Feet sensors detected when weight was lifted, motion sensors detected hip movement and upper-body sensors helped control movement.
Lomas was the first person in the UK to use the ReWalk suit and wore it to complete the 2012 London Marathon in 17 days.
She used it again to complete the Great North Run in 2016, earning the nickname "bionic woman" for her achievements.
Lomas was also selected to light the Paralympic flame in 2012 and was appointed MBE in 2017 for her fundraising efforts.
Before her death Lomas raised Â£925,000 for the Nicholls Spinal Injury Foundation, external - a charity committed to funding research into curing spinal cord injury.
Her husband Dan Spincer and best friend Stuart Hall took the total she raised for charity past Â£1m - and vowed to continue raising money in her memory.
The hearing was not attended by Lomas's family members, because it was "too painful" being so close to the anniversary of her death, her relatives' representative Ben Bradley KC said.
The inquest continues.

Lomas was taking part in a filming project for an Apple headset series called Adventure when the accident occurred. Although her condition initially improved in the hospital, she suffered a sudden deterioration and passed away on 22 August 2024. Lomas was widely known for raising nearly £1m for charity after being left paralysed by a 2007 horse riding accident, notably completing the 2012 London Marathon in a bionic suit.
key_points: Claire Lomas died on August 22, 2024, following a microlight crash in Jordan on July 15 while filming for an Apple series called Adventure.
The coroner stated her provisional cause of death was multiple severe traumatic injuries after she had an infection and sudden deterioration in the hospital.
Lomas became famous for raising nearly £1m for charity, including completing the 2012 London Marathon in a robotic ReWalk suit.
Evidence at the inquest showed there were no mechanical issues with the aircraft or problems with the weather during the flight.
