What remains may be a new point of light, a star that has brightened, an asteroid that has shifted position, an active galaxy that has flickered, or an imaging artifact. For each qualifying change, Rubin can issue a public alert within about two minutes of taking the image.
That is why “alert” should not be read as “emergency” either. Most notifications will concern ordinary but scientifically useful variability. Some objects will generate repeated alerts on different nights. Some signals will already be known. A fraction will be false detections that quality controls and later analysis remove. The seven-million figure describes the scale of a change-detection stream, not seven million wholly new things appearing in the Universe before breakfast.
No person could inspect that stream manually. Rubin sends it to community alert brokers, software services that match detections against catalogues, analyse their light curves and assign possible classifications. Researchers can then ask for a manageable subset: likely young supernovae, fast-moving objects, unusual variable stars, or sources near a recent gravitational-wave location. Rubin’s public guide to the alert stream is unusually clear about the brokers’ role. The telescope notices change; the brokers make that change searchable.
A movie with gaps, filters and revisits
Calling LSST a ten-year time-lapse is helpful so long as we do not imagine an ordinary film. Rubin does not stare continuously at one fixed scene. It moves among fields, uses six broad colour filters over the course of the survey, and revisits a given area according to a carefully optimised schedule. The result is closer to a vast set of interleaved flipbooks than one smooth video.
That structure is scientifically useful. Changes over minutes and days can reveal explosions, flares and moving asteroids. Repeated measurements over months and years show longer cycles, subtle motions and slow changes. Multiple exposures can also be combined, allowing astronomers to pull out objects too faint to stand confidently above the noise in one frame.
Rubin’s early work has already shown how productive that combination can be. During roughly six weeks of optimisation observations, the observatory reported more than 11,000 previously unknown asteroids, including 33 near-Earth objects and 380 trans-Neptunian objects. Space Daily recently covered the first peer-reviewed asteroid study based on LSST Camera data, including an unusually fast-spinning main-belt object found before the main survey had formally started.
Those early totals are evidence that the system works, not a promise of identical discovery counts every six weeks. Survey yield depends on where Rubin looks, observing conditions, object brightness, follow-up work and the definition of a new object. A detection becomes durable knowledge only after its measurements survive checking and, often, confirmation by other observations.
Four programmes sharing one stream of images
Rubin was designed around four broad scientific programmes: cataloguing the Solar System, mapping the Milky Way, exploring the changing sky, and investigating dark matter and dark energy. The same exposure can contribute to more than one of them.
An image taken partly to trace how galaxies are distributed across the Universe can contain an asteroid moving through the foreground. A series used to measure a variable star can also improve a map of the Milky Way. A supernova alert may prompt another telescope to collect a spectrum while Rubin’s archive preserves what the region looked like before the explosion.
The observatory’s name connects its broad survey directly to one of those long-term questions. Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured galaxy rotation in enough detail to show that stars far from galactic centres were moving much faster than visible matter could explain. As our earlier account of Rubin’s rotation-curve work noted, she did not invent the idea of missing mass, but her observations supplied some of its most persuasive evidence. The observatory named for her will approach the problem statistically, using billions of galaxies and repeated measurements of how matter bends light and structures grow.
The telescope includes a trip to California
Rubin collects about ten terabytes of image data each night. That material travels from Chile to the US Data Facility at SLAC in California for initial processing. Software must calibrate the images, compare them with templates, construct alerts and distribute the results quickly enough for other observatories to respond while a short-lived event is still visible.
Seen this way, the telescope does not end at the mountaintop. The fibre links, processing centres, databases and alert brokers are as necessary to time-domain astronomy as the mirror and camera. Without them, Rubin would still take extraordinary images, but the fastest and most temporary events could remain buried until their useful follow-up window had closed.
The arrangement also changes who can take part. Rubin’s world-public alerts can be accessed through its broker network, while larger processed datasets will arrive through scheduled releases. Access to data does not erase the need for computing skill, telescope time or institutional resources, but it distributes the starting material far more widely than an observatory whose images remain with one small team.
The real instrument is repetition
The easiest detail to remember is the car-sized camera. The most consequential number may be 800, the approximate number of visits each point in the survey will accumulate. A single image tells astronomers what was visible. A long, consistently measured sequence can show what changed, when it changed and whether it changed before.
That is where Rubin may be most valuable. The rare supernova caught minutes after appearing will make a fine headline. So will an asteroid passing unusually close to Earth or a distant object behaving in a way no catalogue predicted. But many of the survey’s strongest results will emerge from the ordinary nights between those moments, when the telescope repeats the same disciplined work and extends the baseline by another 40 seconds, another visit, another season.
Rubin is often presented as a machine for finding what nobody has seen. It is also a machine for remembering what the sky looked like before anything seemed important. In astronomy, where the decisive event may happen once and fade before anyone knows to look, that memory is a form of discovery in its own right.

Rubin Observatory in Chile officially launched its ten-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time on June 30, 2026, using a car-sized, 3,200-megapixel camera. The observatory captures a new image of the southern sky roughly every 40 seconds, aiming to build a comprehensive time-lapse record and issue millions of nightly alerts for detected changes. This massive stream of data will help astronomers track asteroids, map the Milky Way, and study dark matter, dark energy, and dynamic cosmic events.

The observatory captures approximately a thousand images per night, revisiting every point in its survey footprint about 800 times over ten years.
Rubin can issue up to seven million change-detection alerts per night within about two minutes of taking an image.
Data gathered from the survey supports four main scientific programmes: cataloguing the Solar System, mapping the Milky Way, exploring the changing sky, and investigating dark matter and dark energy.

fe5d731e2cd67830493f13f2.title: You can call ADHD whatever you like — I still have to live with it
fe5d731e2cd67830493f13f2.author: Jessica Lindsay
fe5d731e2cd67830493f13f2.content:
![Max Pemberton on The Great ADHD Myth?](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/image003-4ab6.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
In Channel 4’s new documentary, The Great ADHD Myth?, psychiatrist Max Pemberton seeks to determine whether it’s ‘a genuine neurodevelopmental disorder, or a social construct.’
Having spent the five years since my own diagnosis fielding similar bad faith questions — and given Pemberton has previously suggested that ADHD could be a ‘wildly overdiagnosed’ ‘fad’ — the resulting answer didn’t come as a shock.
Despite claiming to take a ‘science-led approach’, the show appeared to use the same carefully-chosen sceptics and cherry-picked evidence as every other so-called investigation into the ‘rise’ of neurodiversity.
It’s all pretty inflammatory.
One of the experts featured called medication prescribed to treat ADHD ‘slow-release cocaine’ (as someone who’s taken both, I can confirm that’s complete nonsense), while others said it was ‘worse’ than corporal punishment or likened it to chemical castration.
What felt especially unique about the documentary though, is how it merged these provocative statements with elements of truth, latching their central thesis onto legitimate concerns about everything from big pharma to ultra-processed foods to smartphone addiction.
Personally, I’m inclined to trust the World Health Organization, the NHS and NICE in their classifications of ADHD as a lifelong neurodevelopmental disorder.
But let’s for a minute assume Max Pemberton and co are correct and it is in fact a product of modern society — when people are suffering, who’s helped by proving that point?
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/GettyImages-925684848-3e6d.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
The thread that runs through the hour-long show is an experiment where a 10-year-old boy with ADHD, Mason, is taken off his meds in favour of daily yoga, woodland walks, diet changes and screen time limits.
Ask Metro
Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.
During the four-week trial, we’re told he’d become ‘more fun’ and ‘a proper character’.
When his teacher reports that the year 6 pupil is struggling to concentrate or regulate his emotions during lessons, and was ‘easier to teach’ while medicated, it’s labelled as an ‘educational issue’.
At the end, Mason whoops with joy as his mum Shauna decides to keep him off the drugs for a longer period to avoid ‘dulling his sparkle to suit everyone else’.
It’s not until the credits roll that we find out he’s back on them after doing poorly in his exams.
In Pemberton’s view, this experiment (with the smallest possible sample size of one) raised some ‘profound philosophical and moral questions’ about neurodiversity.
In mine, it’s a clear example of the real world harms that can come from constantly questioning its very existence.
Ex-GP Iona Heath said on the show that if she was in charge, she’d ‘ban the label ADHD, straight off.’
‘I would stop medicating this group of people, then I would absolutely want to overhaul the education system for children to include many more creative activities and sporting activities,’ she added.
‘I think that would reveal an untapped reservoir of talent that we are currently drugging out of existence.’
Cool. If I could bake a cake filled with rainbows and smiles, everyone would eat it and be happy.
Until we build that utopia, Mason has to follow a set curriculum alongside the 30-odd other kids in his class in order to get the qualifications he needs to be a functioning member of society.
And I, along with the millions of adults with ADHD who work in offices, have to sit at a desk and concentrate for eight hours a day to earn a living.
![](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/GettyImages-2148402031-9f6b.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
It’s not that I don’t agree with any of the points raised in the documentary around how modernity and diagnoses seem to go hand in hand. In fact, I’m a firm believer that in another time, or even a less rigid class system, the hyperfocus and creativity of neurodivergence would be seen as assets rather than problems.
I’m sure our collective need for instant gratification isn’t helping the symptoms of ADHD either, and we could all benefit from touching a little more grass, eating a little less sugar, and spending a lot less time doomscrolling.
The reality of life today, though, is that we rely on phones to do most things, from taxes to communicating with loved ones, working long hours at increasingly insecure jobs, often in built-up areas.
- 
	![Woman massaging her leg because of leg muscle cramps. Muscle pain or leg pain while sleeping in the bed. High quality photo](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308652563-f573.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646&h=363&crop=1)
- A man at church told me about his fetish — now I fulfil his fantasy for £120 an hour
- This is what Brits consider cheating — men and women have very different views
- Your star sign's daily horoscope for August 19, 2026
If you want to get by in a world where productivity is king, you need to conform to a certain extent. For those of us with ADHD, medication is the most accessible way to do that.
Perhaps, as Pemberton concludes, it is ‘dystopian’ to medicate children (albeit with drugs that have been safely used for decades) and to medicalise ‘normal’ behaviour instead of changing the society that deems it otherwise.
What scares me more is that research shows someone with diagnosed ADHD has a seven to nine-year lower life expectancy, not to mention a higher risk of substance abuse issues, unemployment and even suicide.
That is the reality we are doing our best to deal with in the here and now. Thinking that arguing the semantics of our condition or demonising medication many of us find life-changing will help improve our situation would be the biggest myth of all.

acd72b53f060c6c5fbbd4acf.title: London’s first official bathing area hit by toxic algae outbreak
acd72b53f060c6c5fbbd4acf.author: Maryam Zakir-Hussain
acd72b53f060c6c5fbbd4acf.content:
London’s first official bathing spot has been hit by a toxic algal bloom, as swimmers have been warned to avoid the river.
The Ham and Kingston site on the Thames became a bathing spot as recently as May this year.
However, the Environment Agency (EA) issued a formal notice on Tuesday cautioning against swimming, warning: “Bathing is not advised, due to pollution from harmful algae.”
Staff from the regulator have taken samples of the water since May, checking for harmful bacteria and to establish the water quality.
Marlene Lawrence, who founded local swimming group Teddington Bluetits said swam in the river before the warning notice was issued.
![London ’s Ham and Kingston on the Thames has been hit by a toxic algal bloom](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/13/07/PA-85591021-3b704fb8.jpeg)
“Instantly on Sunday night I came out in a really bad rash, itchy spots, and that’s not like me. I can only attribute it to the algae in the river,” she told The Times.
The semi-retired swimmer, who helped secure the site as a bathing spot, first noticed signs of algae last week.
She believes the consecutive record-breaking heatwaves are behind the water pollution.
According to the EA, during an algal bloom, the water becomes less clear and may become blue-green or greenish-brown.
Scums can form during calm weather when several bloom-forming species rise to the surface. This can look like paint, mousse or small clumps.
Cyanobacteria or ‘blue-green algae’, a type of blooming algae, can produce toxins. These toxins can kill wild animals, livestock and pets. They can also harm people, producing rashes after skin contact and illnesses if swallowed.
An Environment Agency spokesperson said: “We have identified blue-green algae on the lower River Thames including the Ham and Kingston designated bathing water.
“We are working with the Royal Borough of Kingston upon Thames, who have put signage in this location to warn people that it is not safe to swim.
“An advice against bathing notice has been activated on the Swiminfo website.”
The spokesperson also warned that it was likely the section of the River Thames between Hampton and Kingston had also been affected.
“It is important that members of public do not enter the Thames along this stretch. It is also vitally important to keep dogs out of the water,” they urged.
![Cyanobacteria or ‘blue-green algae’, a type of blooming algae, can produce toxins](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/13/18/PA-76925632-92d43734.jpeg)
It comes as a sobering new assessment has revealed that a mere 14 per cent of England’s rivers, lakes, and coastal waters are currently in good ecological health.
The findings come from the Environment Agency’s first update in six years, conducted under retained EU legislation governing water quality.
This comprehensive evaluation scrutinised 4,658 of the country’s rivers, lakes, estuaries, canals, and coastal waters, measuring their health against a range of standards including wildlife populations, overall water quality, and the condition of physical habitats.
The report indicates that just 14.3 per cent of surface water bodies achieved an overall good ecological status in 2025, with widespread issues attributed to sewage spills, agricultural nutrient runoff, and pollutants emanating from urban areas and roads, such as litter, petrol, and garden pesticides.

Swimmers have reported rashes following contact with the water, and authorities have urged people and dogs to stay out of the affected stretch between Hampton and Kingston. The incident coincides with a broader Environment Agency assessment revealing that only 14.3 per cent of England's surface waters achieved good ecological status in 2025.
key_points: The Environment Agency issued a formal warning advising against swimming at London's first official bathing site in Ham and Kingston due to toxic blue-green algae.
Local swimmers have reported developing rashes and itchy spots after entering the water before the warning was issued.
Authorities have erected warning signs and advised the public to keep both themselves and their dogs out of the affected stretch of the Thames.
A recent Environment Agency assessment reported that only 14.3 per cent of England's rivers, lakes, and coastal waters are currently in good ecological health.

This comprehensive evaluation scrutinised 4,658 of the country’s rivers, lakes, estuaries, canals, and coastal waters, measuring their health against a range of standards including wildlife populations, overall water quality, and the condition of physical habitats.
The report indicates that just 14.3 per cent of surface water bodies achieved an overall good ecological status in 2025, with widespread issues attributed to sewage spills, agricultural nutrient runoff, and pollutants emanating from urban areas and roads, such as litter, petrol, and garden pesticides.
7f146611a32cccb11a90dde2.summary: London's first official bathing spot at Ham and Kingston on the Thames has been hit by a toxic blue-green algal bloom, prompting warnings from the Environment Agency advising the public not to swim. Swimmers have reported rashes following contact with the water, and authorities have urged people and dogs to stay out of the affected stretch between Hampton and Kingston. The incident coincides with a broader Environment Agency assessment revealing that only 14.3 per cent of England's surface waters achieved good ecological status in 2025.
key_points: The Environment Agency issued a formal warning advising against swimming at London's first official bathing site in Ham and Kingston due to toxic blue-green algae.
Local swimmers have reported developing rashes and itchy spots after entering the water before the warning was issued.
Authorities have erected warning signs and advised the public to keep both themselves and their dogs out of the affected stretch of the Thames.
A recent Environment Agency assessment reported that only 14.3 per cent of England's rivers, lakes, and coastal waters are currently in good ecological health.

7b07cbab4703782e06c7ccb1.title: Russia is threatening escalation against Britain: Here’s how they could do it
7b07cbab4703782e06c7ccb1.author: David Blair; Roland Oliphant
7b07cbab4703782e06c7ccb1.content:
“You send a message that you are capable of penetrating a Western airport and Western Europe, and potentially it might be extremely damaging, but you stop short of causing any real damage. That would serve the purpose, because the purpose we have seen since 2022 in Russian sabotage operations was always to raise the costs of supplying support to Ukraine and raising the costs of protecting critical infrastructure.”
Given that Russia is also doubtless seeking to divide British society and stir up as much trouble as possible, there are plenty of other methods that have already been tried elsewhere. In France, Russian agents have variously deposited pigs’ heads outside mosques, defaced synagogues and vandalised the country’s Holocaust memorial. They even left mock coffins under the Eiffel Tower. The French government has also blamed Russia for trying to frighten tourists away from Paris by spreading the story in 2023 that the city’s hotels were infected with bed bugs.
Many of those operations could be traced back to a Russian company called the Social Design Agency, which is close to the Kremlin, according to leaked documents published by Delfi, an Estonian news website.
Last month, British police officials warned that both Russia and Iran were trying their best to inflame social conflict. “Their ultimate goal is destabilising our democracy, sowing division and chaos, and disturbing our peace,” said Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing.
Assassinate Britons inside Britain
Likelihood: Medium
Russian intelligence has a long record of murdering – or trying to murder – people on British soil. But, so far, the targets have always been Russian exiles whom the Kremlin would consider traitors. The former spy Alexander Litvinenko, for instance, suffered an agonising death in 2006 when two Russian agents poisoned him with radioactive polonium in a London hotel. Later, in 2018, two GRU officers attempted to kill Sergei Skripal, a Russian defector, with Novichok nerve agent in Salisbury. Skripal survived, but his erstwhile assassins carelessly discarded their lethal substance, which killed Dawn Sturgess, an innocent British mother of three.
If Russia wished to escalate, it could expand its target list to include British citizens involved in arming Ukraine. Once again, events in Germany may provide a guide. In 2024, the CIA uncovered a Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, the chief executive of Rheinmetall, the German defence giant.
His British counterpart would be Charles Woodburn, the chief executive of BAE Systems, the biggest British defence company and a supplier of advanced drones to Ukraine. But Woodburn – and others like him – will presumably be well-protected against any threat.
Indeed, killing people in Britain might be harder than doing so elsewhere in Europe. “It should not be completely ruled out, but Britain has built experience because of the Litvinenko and Skripal cases,” says Katia Glod, the deputy head of foreign policy at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre. “It’s harder to do that in Britain today than in Germany or France, which are probably more penetrated by [Russian] spies.”
Attack British facilities in Ukraine
Likelihood: High
This is probably the most likely option for any Russian escalation. Britain’s effort to supply Ukraine relies on a network of physical facilities inside that country. The existence of some has been publicly disclosed. In March, the Ministry of Defence said there were four “maintenance, repair and overhaul” facilities in Ukraine, where “UK companies with British and Ukrainian workforces” were engaged in reconditioning armoured fighting vehicles and artillery.
BAE Systems, meanwhile, announced in 2023 that it was establishing a “local presence” inside Ukraine. If Russia knows where any of these facilities are located, striking them with missiles or drones – and probably killing any Britons working inside them – would be a straightforward way of retaliating against Britain.
“They probably would try to start with something on Ukrainian territory,” says Soldatov. “They are actually quite creative at identifying what belongs to which country in Ukraine, so they might attack some facilities which they think might have some connections to Britain.”
What about British diplomatic premises, such as the embassy in Kyiv? Russia is less likely to take that step because it has plenty of embassies of its own and therefore retains an interest in preserving the immunity of diplomatic premises.
As for the drones that Britain is sending to Ukraine for long-range strikes on Russia, one option would be to target them as soon as they enter the country. Moskovsky Komsomolets, a Russian daily, recently pointed out that the drones in question are delivered as finished products and suggested targeting the containers the moment they crossed the border into Ukraine. That would require precise intelligence about the timing of drone consignments and the exact lorries in which they are carried.
Whether the Russians have acquired such detailed information is unknown. If they have, using this intelligence to destroy the British-supplied drones before they can take off would be the most logical response.
Direct military strikes on Britain with missiles or armed drones
Likelihood: Low
As Ukrainian attacks cripple oil refineries, giant warehouses and arms factories across Russia, the Kremlin must be sorely tempted to hit back against one of its enemy’s principal allies. At this moment, almost everywhere in Europe and particularly in Britain, advanced weapons are being made for Ukraine to use against Russian soldiers on the frontline and increasingly against targets in Russia itself.
Tempting but still unlikely. With its force bogged down in Ukraine and its arms-making capacity stretched to the limit, the last thing that Russia needs is to provoke a retaliatory attack from Nato. If a Russian missile or drone were to slam into a British arms factory, killing scores or hundreds of people inside, the danger is that Britain might invoke Article V, the mutual defence clause of the Nato treaty, and Putin’s difficulties would suddenly become even greater.
“I don’t think the military logic would allow that option,” says Glod. “I don’t think the Kremlin discounts the possibility of a Nato kinetic strike back and it wouldn’t be able to counter that because of its stretched military production.”
Despite the blood-curdling words of the Russian embassy in London – though it is notable that the threatening statement did not come from a higher level, such as the foreign ministry in Moscow or the Kremlin itself – the most likely outcome is that Russia will step up the existing campaign against Britain. Its operatives will probably do more of the same, running the gamut of sabotage, drone incursions, cyber attacks and disinformation, while staying just below the level of triggering open armed conflict.
“In many ways,” says Galeotti, referring to the embassy statement, “the language is an expression of impotence because, yes, Putin does have escalatory options, but they all have massive costs and risks for Russia.”
7b07cbab4703782e06c7ccb1.summary: Russia is considering potential escalations against Britain to raise the costs of supporting Ukraine and to destabilize British society through operations such as sabotage and disinformation. While methods like hybrid warfare, attacks on British facilities in Ukraine, or targeting UK-supplied weapons are possible, direct military strikes on Britain remain unlikely due to the risk of triggering NATO's mutual defense clause. Consequently, Russia is expected to continue utilizing covert tactics like sabotage and cyber attacks that remain just below the threshold of open armed conflict.
key_points: Russian sabotage and influence operations aim to raise the costs of supporting Ukraine and sow division in Western societies.
Potential escalation tactics include targeting British citizens involved in arming Ukraine or attacking British maintenance and repair facilities located within Ukraine.
Direct military strikes on British soil are considered unlikely because they risk triggering NATO's Article V mutual defense clause.
Russia is most likely to intensify its existing campaign of sabotage, drone incursions, cyber attacks, and disinformation.

d79d21a776516b33216ce5a5.title: Natalie Harp stowed in trunk of SUV when Trump’s motorcade had no space: report
d79d21a776516b33216ce5a5.author: Owen Scott
d79d21a776516b33216ce5a5.content:
The estranged brother of Natalie Harp, Donald Trump’s doting aide, struggled to contain his laughter when told of the reported lengths his sister went to accompany Trump to a court hearing.
Preston Harp initially burst out laughing when CNN’s Erin Burnett asked for his reaction to the network’s report that his sister jumped into the trunk of an SUV when there wasn’t space for her to ride in Trump’s motorcade on the way to a court hearing in New York City in October 2023.
The network reports that a “screaming match” took place in the lobby of Trump Tower after there was no room for Natalie Harp in the motorcade. The aide reportedly insisted she had been asked by Trump to attend the hearing, but with no seat available, she climbed into the trunk of an SUV, according to sources and a photograph seen by CNN.
“That's really funny, I didn't know about that,” Preston Harp told CNN's Erin Burnett OutFront through laughter.
Burnett then asked him, “You're laughing, but I mean, is it funny or what? You know her, so that's why...”
![Preston Harp initially burst out laughing when CNN’s Erin Burnett asked for his reaction to the network’s report](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/19/14/22/preston-harp.png)
“No, it’s not, I'm sorry, it’s actually sad,” Preston Harp added. “That’s obsession. That’s like an unhealthy obsession with someone if you’re going to jump into the trunk of their car.”
Natalie Harp’s estranged sibling, a Trump critic, also detailed more about his upbringing with his sister, claiming that his mom believed in American exceptionalism.
“Trump is like everything that my mom taught us to respect,” he said. “I think that's where her infatuation with Trump comes from, honestly.”
The reported trunk incident is another example of Natalie Harp’s devotion to the president, which has “unnerved” some of her White House colleagues, according to The New York Times.
She has come under the spotlight this week, with multiple reports detailing how she became one of his most trusted supporters. The executive assistant is often seen by the president’s side, having cultivated a close working relationship since she first came to Trump’s attention in 2019.
She joined Trump’s staff in 2022, having claimed he “saved her life” after she was diagnosed with stage II bone cancer. She hit the headlines earlier this month when it emerged she was one of a small number of aides who were transferred to a military plane in Turkey to avoid a suspected assassination threat by Iran.
One unnamed White House advisor told CNN that Trump “likes the attention and the fact that she is 100 percent committed and loyal.”
“She doesn’t second-guess, doesn’t question,” the advisor said of Natalie Harp, who has also reportedly earned the nickname of “human printer” for handing the president hard copies of social media posts and newspaper articles.
Democratic senator Jon Ossoff drew further attention to Natalie Harp this week after suggesting at a rally Trump would rather fly with “Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace” than do his job.
The Trump administration has vociferously defended her, with the official Rapid Response 47 account on X tearing into a CNN correspondent who asked the president about the aide.
She was described as “one of the most loyal and hardest working aides on President Trump’s team” in a statement by White House spokesman Davis Ingle this week.
And Ossoff, meanwhile, was branded a “radical, extremist Dumocrat” by White House communications director Steven Cheung in a social media response to his speech.
d79d21a776516b33216ce5a5.summary: Donald Trump aide Natalie Harp reportedly climbed into the trunk of an SUV during an October 2023 motorcade in New York City after discovering there was no room for her to ride inside. Her estranged brother, Preston Harp, reacted to the report by calling it an unhealthy obsession, while administration officials have strongly defended her loyalty and hard work. Harp is known for her close devotion to Trump, having joined his staff in 2022 after previously crediting him with saving her life.
key_points: Natalie Harp reportedly climbed into the trunk of an SUV to accompany Donald Trump to an October 2023 court hearing when no seats were available in the motorcade.
Her estranged brother, Preston Harp, initially laughed at the report before describing her behavior as an unhealthy obsession.
White House officials and a spokesperson strongly defended Harp, describing her as one of the president's most loyal and hardworking aides.
Harp joined Trump's staff in 2022 after previously stating that he saved her life following her bone cancer diagnosis.

aff2a27b4370c240b00c70af.title: All power to the UK competition watchdog’s war on ‘drip pricing’
aff2a27b4370c240b00c70af.author: Nils Pratley
aff2a27b4370c240b00c70af.content:
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is on-message with Andy Burnham’s declaration of war on the small – and sometimes not-so-small – hassles and expenses of everyday consumer life created by companies’ underhand and misleading pricing tactics. Trainline, Virgin Atlantic and Red Driving School found themselves under investigation on Wednesday for various forms of alleged “drip pricing” – not being upfront about mandatory add-on charges, in other words.
The prime minister had nothing to do with the CMA’s pursuit, it should be said. The watchdog’s “consumer protection drive” pre-dates his arrival and was encouraged by legislation under the last Tory government – the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act of 2024, which gave the regulator “direct enforcement” powers, meaning it no longer had to go to court under consumer protection laws. And it is using those powers: eight cases were opened last November and driving schools AA and BSM plus the ticketing site StubHub UK have already been fined.
This is very welcome. Putting a few household names in the spotlight sends a usefully strong message. By way of boosting that signal, shares in Trainline, the only quoted company on Wednesday’s list, plunged by 14%.
![A Virgin Atlantic plane taxis on a runway](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/5576ba431ec0e73059f2de2e82fc32c2c6f38bef/171_0_2715_2173/master/2715.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
It’s merely an investigation at this stage, so one can’t draw conclusions, but there was a curious line in Trainline’s statement. “Trainline has proactively engaged with the CMA over several months and is taking steps to enhance the presentation of certain fees,” it said.
The obvious question is why, if the regulator has been on the warpath for months, Trainline didn’t just give it everything it wanted on day one. Regular users of the slick app know there can be a fee at the end of the booking process (for about 30% of journeys), so they are unlikely to be deterred by a message to that effect displayed prominently at the outset.
There may be complicating details. Trainline adds its value for consumers by navigating the hellishly complicated fare structures on Britain’s railways by, for example, identifying so-called “split tickets” (multiple tickets covering legs of a single journey) or cases where an obscure railcard will almost pay for itself. If Trainline’s fee depends on the type of ticket, perhaps it’s not possible to state the fee precisely until the punter has chosen.
But such dry technicalities were, presumably, mentioned in the months of engagement with the CMA. So it would be fair for Trainline shareholders to ask how this affair has even reached the stage of a formal investigation by a regulator with the power to order refunds and fine 10% of turnover. It’s not as if large sums are involved – the CMA said it observed transactions with additional fees ranging from 50p to £2.79.
after newsletter promotion
To repeat, no wrongdoing has been found. But the investigation comes at a bad moment as Trainline waits to see if the state, in the form of the new Great British Railways, gets round to launching a rival fee-free ticketing app. A regulatory quarrel over transparency is the last thing it needs.
aff2a27b4370c240b00c70af.summary: The UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has launched investigations into Trainline, Virgin Atlantic, and Red Driving School over alleged "drip pricing" tactics regarding mandatory add-on charges. Utilizing direct enforcement powers granted by the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act of 2024, the watchdog aims to crack down on misleading consumer pricing. Following the announcement, Trainline's shares plunged by 14% as the company faces a formal inquiry despite previously engaging with the regulator.
key_points: The CMA is investigating Trainline, Virgin Atlantic, and Red Driving School for alleged drip pricing.
The watchdog is utilizing direct enforcement powers provided by the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act of 2024.
Trainline's shares fell by 14% following the announcement of the investigation.
Trainline stated it had been proactively engaging with the CMA over several months regarding fee presentation.

So it would be fair for Trainline shareholders to ask how this affair has even reached the stage of a formal investigation by a regulator with the power to order refunds and fine 10% of turnover. It’s not as if large sums are involved – the CMA said it observed transactions with additional fees ranging from 50p to £2.79.
after newsletter promotion
To repeat, no wrongdoing has been found. But the investigation comes at a bad moment as Trainline waits to see if the state, in the form of the new Great British Railways, gets round to launching a rival fee-free ticketing app. A regulatory quarrel over transparency is the last thing it needs.
0c0516c265321357d286ba31.summary: The UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has launched investigations into Trainline, Virgin Atlantic, and Red Driving School over alleged "drip pricing" tactics regarding mandatory add-on charges. Utilizing direct enforcement powers granted by the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act of 2024, the watchdog aims to crack down on misleading consumer pricing. Following the announcement, Trainline's shares plunged by 14% as the company faces a formal inquiry despite previously engaging with the regulator.

The watchdog is utilizing direct enforcement powers provided by the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act of 2024.
Trainline's shares fell by 14% following the announcement of the investigation.

334cb5fa7f7f1970511cb6c8.title: Hayden Panettiere latest: Heroes star’s on-off boyfriend was present at death scene
334cb5fa7f7f1970511cb6c8.author: Jacob Stolworthy; Shahana Yasmin; Caitlin Hornik
334cb5fa7f7f1970511cb6c8.content:
Hayden Panettiere, who became a household name as a teenager for her role in Heroes and later starred in Nashville and multiple Scream films, has died at age 36.
Panettiere was pronounced dead at a South Carolina apartment Sunday, August 16. A cause of death has not been revealed, but an autopsy showed no signs of trauma. Toxicology reports are pending and could take up to 12 weeks, according to the Greenville County Coroner’s Office.
A newly released incident report states that the 911 call was made by Brian Hickerson, 37, who is referred to as Panettiere’s boyfriend. He eportedly turned over a “bag of medication” belonging to Panettiere to the police, but the contents of that bag has so far been redacted. His brother Zach Hickerson was also present on the scene. The Independent has approached police for further information.
The actor’s father, Skip, confirmed Panettiere’s death in a heartbreaking statement to ABC News. Panettiere’s ex-fiance, Wladimir Klitschko said he was “deeply saddened” by the news but vowed to make sure the couple’s daughter, Kaya, “remembers the person” Panettiere was.
Dozens of Panettiere’s co-stars including Heroes actor Masi Oka, Nashville co-star Connie Britton, Tim Allen, Viola Davis and Melissa Barrera have offered heartfelt tributes to the two-time Golden Globe nominee on social media.
Among her most memorable roles were Sheryl Yoast in the 2000 Denzel Washington-led film Remember the Titans, high school cheerleader Claire Bennet on NBC’s sci-fi drama Heroes (2006-2010), and aspiring country singer Juliette Barnes on the hit TV series Nashville (2012-2018).
Her New York Times bestselling memoir, This Is Me: A Reckoning, was published in May this year, in which she looked back at her childhood in Hollywood and her experiences with addiction, postpartum depression, abusive relationships, and the loss of custody of her daughter, Kaya, whom she shares with former heavyweight boxer Wladimir Klitschko.
Hayden Panettiere dead: Heroes and Nashville star dies aged 36
Hayden Panettiere, best known for her roles in Heroes, Nashville, and the Scream franchise, has died aged 36.
“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of our beloved Hayden,” Panettiere’s father, Skip said in a statement to ABC News. “She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her — and to the millions who watched her onscreen.”
No cause of death was announced.
![Hayden Panettiere attends Jony And Marc's (RED) Auction at Sotheby's in New York](https://static.the-independent.com/2026/08/17/04/2026-08-17T031938Z_1937106696_RC230NATJBN1_RTRMADP_3_PEOPLE-HAYDEN-PANETTIERE.JPG)
Wladimir Klitschko breaks silence over ex-fiancée's death
In an Instagram post, Wladimir Klitschko wrote: “Our family is going through a time of profound shock and grief.
“The announcement of Hayden’s tragic death saddens me deeply. She left this world far too soon. Hayden was, although no longer my partner, an important part of my life and the mother of our daughter, Kaya.
“She built an incredible career through immense talent, while also facing the darker sides of a very demanding industry. Nothing will erase the times we shared or the place she had in our lives.
“To our daughter Kaya, I will always speak of her mother with respect and make sure she remembers the person she was.
“I extend my deepest condolences to Hayden’s parents, her friends, and her fans, who are also grieving today. Young and talented people like Hayden should not leave this world so soon.
“I ask everyone to please respect our family’s feelings and privacy during this incredibly difficult time. For now, this is all I wish to say.
“Thank you to everyone who is supporting my family and expressing their sincere condolences.
“Rest easy, Hayden. May you find eternal peace. #WeLoveYouHayden”
Panettiere still struggled with decades-old injuries
In her 2026 memoir, This Is Me: A Reckoning, Panettiere recalled being thrown from a zebra while filming the 2005 movie, Racing Stripes.
Just 14 years old at the time, Panettiere suffered damage to two vertebrae in her neck, a concussion and severe whiplash.
“I kept my mouth shut and endured the pain in my back and neck,” she wrote in her memoir.
“Over 20 years later, these injuries still bother me.”
Cops spotted at Hickerson family home days after Panettiere's death
Police have been spotted at a Hickerson family residence about five miles from where Panettiere died Sunday.
Her on-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach were both with her when she died.
Now, Page Six reported Wednesday that cops were seen outside a home belonging to the Hickerson brothers’ grandmother.
A pair of officers were seen around 8:20 a.m. ET knocking on front and side doors of the residence. They returned about 90 minutes later to “conduct a welfare check,” the outlet reported.
However, it was not clear who the intended target of the welfare check was.
The Independent has contacted the Greenville Police Department for more information.
Panettiere's 'Heroes' co-star says she 'knew every crew member’s name'
Sendhil Ramamurthy, who starred alongside the late actor on the NBC show Heroes, recalled Panettiere’s kindness.
“I learned a lot from her. She stuck up for background actors when they were mistreated, knew every crew member’s name, and was so generous with her time,” Ramamurthy wrote on Instagram.
“Sending love to her family, friends, and my fellow cast mates, RIP Hayd. You will be missed.”
Steven Tyler pays tribute to his 'dear friend'
The Aerosmith rocker and Panettiere partnered for a duet of the Patsy Cline song “Crazy” for a 2015 episode of Nashville.
Filmmaker recalls Panettiere's on-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson being on movie set
Filmmaker Griff Furst worked with Panettiere on A Breed Apart, which was released in theaters in May 2025.
In an Instagram video shared August 17, Furst recalled Panettiere’s on-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson being on set.
“I had met Hayden about 10 years before that and I knew that she was insanely talented, so when she signed on to do this picture that we were shooting, I was psyched. I really wanted to work with her. So I’m on set, and I get word from the movie’s security team who picked her up from the airport that something was off,” Furst said in the video.
“I didn’t think much about it, and so I left set and I walked over to greet her and her boyfriend Brian. He opened the door. Hayden was incredibly sweet and gracious and excited to work, but she was not okay,” he continued.
“I’m not going to get into the details of why that was, but having worked on over 100 movies and seeing just about everything, it was pretty clear that she wasn’t okay and the energy in her room was pretty dark.”
Baseball star's ties to Panettiere resurface
MLB star Pete Crow-Armstrong comes from a family of actors, including his mom, Ashley Crow, who played Hayden Panettiere’s mother on the hit NBC show Heroes.
The Chicago Cubs center fielder confessed his affection for Panettiere to NBC Chicago in a 2022 interview.
“Hayden Panettiere babysat me. I had the biggest crush on her,” Crow-Armstrong said. “Yeah, I’d say she was probably the coolest one for me.
“I liked being around the older actors, and I liked being babysat by my mom’s co-stars and whatnot.”
Jay Shetty is 'devastated and heartbroken' over Panettiere
Podcaster Shetty shared a tribute on social media Tuesday, months after he sat with Panettiere for what would turn out to be one of her final interviews.
“I’ve been devastated and heartbroken since I heard the news. I’m in shock and have been processing for the past day on your legacy and our loss,” he wrote.
“Just a few months ago, I had the privilege of sitting down with you on On Purpose. After the episode you told me it was truly healing. You said I was now like a big brother to you and that I helped you be brave,” he continued.
“But Hayden, you were the brave one. You were courageous, resilient, and so incredibly strong through so many difficult moments in your life. You should never have had to experience the things you did.”
Hayden Panettiere said she had 'a lot of life left to live'
In one of her last interviews with podcaster Jay Shetty in the months before her death, Hayden Panettiere spoke about her future with hope.

An autopsy showed no signs of trauma, and the cause of death remains pending toxicological reports. Her on-off boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, and his brother were present at the scene when she passed away. Numerous co-stars and public figures have shared tributes honoring her life and career.

An autopsy revealed no signs of trauma, and toxicology results are pending.
Her on-off boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, made the 911 call and was present at the scene with his brother Zach.
Panettiere was widely known for her roles in Heroes, Nashville, and the Scream film franchise.
Her father, Skip Panettiere, and ex-fiancé, Wladimir Klitschko, both released statements mourning her death.

9d60bc3c29c0c5cf1d6a63b6.title: Nick Kyrgios: Controversial tennis player's career could be over after positive cocaine test
9d60bc3c29c0c5cf1d6a63b6.author: Russell Fuller
9d60bc3c29c0c5cf1d6a63b6.content:
![Nick Kyrgios gestures after a point in the Wimbledon men's singles final in 2022](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/71a2/live/4841ebf0-9be2-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Nick Kyrgios has won seven ATP Tour singles titles
- Published
Nick Kyrgios once said there was "zero chance" he would be playing tennis into his 30s.
But it was at the age of 31, while attempting another comeback from serious knee and wrist injuries, that he tested positive for a metabolite of cocaine at June's Mallorca Open.
In a post on social media, Kyrgios said it was a "huge mistake" for which he takes full responsibility.
But he added that recent injuries - he has only played eight tournaments and won two matches since the start of 2023 - have taken a huge toll on him.
"Coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined," he added.
Kyrgios will not be able to play until his case is resolved because of a mandatory provisional suspension.
But although he faces a potential ban of up to four years, his suspension would be limited to a maximum of three months if he can prove the drug was taken out of competition.
Kyrgios suspended after positive cocaine test
The Australian has achieved more than most on the sporting stage. As a 19-year-old in 2014 he stunned then world number one Rafael Nadal on his Centre Court debut, and finished runner-up at Wimbledon eight years later.
At his best, Kyrgios is a flamboyant and athletic shot-maker with flair, touch and an explosive game.
But he can also be destructive and verbally abusive, and has regularly struggled to sustain the levels of professionalism and abstinence needed for a prolonged stay at the very top.
In 2015, Kyrgios was given a suspended 28-day ban for making lewd remarks about Stan Wawrinka's girlfriend during a match in Montreal.
A year later, he was banned for eight weeks for his behaviour - including a "lack of best effort" - at the Shanghai Masters. This was reduced to three weeks after he agreed to consult a sports psychologist.
2019 was the nadir. Kyrgios was defaulted from a match at the Italian Open for hurling a chair on to the court, and was later fined $113,000 for verbally abusing umpire Fergus Murphy in Cincinnati.
The ATP later issued a suspended 16-week ban for a "pattern of behaviour related to his verbal abuse of officials and/or spectators" over the previous 12 months.
![Nick Kyrgios walks off with the Wimbledon singles runner-up trophy after losing the 2022 final to Novak Djokovic](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/a2d0/live/08e2d5b0-9bdc-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Nick Kyrgios reached his sole Grand Slam singles final at Wimbledon in 2022, losing to Novak Djokovic
Kyrgios described 2019 as the "lowest point of my career" when interviewed for Netflix's Break Point documentary series.
"I was drinking, abusing drugs. I lost my relationship with my family, pushed all my close friends away," he said.
"Being bullied at a young age for being short and fat and brown scarred me for sure."
Kyrgios said he wore a compression sleeve to cover up self-harming scars on his arm and spent time in a psychiatric hospital in London to try and "figure out my problems".
He separately spoke about being forced out of a pub in Wimbledon Village by his agent in the early hours of a match day, and told Louis Theroux in 2024 that he would sometimes have "20 to 30 drinks" before playing the next day.
He has confessed to playing too much basketball - including for an hour before he beat David Ferrer in the 2017 Cincinnati Masters semi-finals - and has often said he has been unable to "dedicate" his life to tennis.
"I just enjoy doing whatever I'm doing," he said.
"I don't eat well. I don't train just for tennis, I train just for a general happy living - I know it sounds ridiculous, but I play a bit of tennis on the side."
![Nick Kyrgios and Thanasi Kokkinakis pose after winning the Australian Open men's doubles title in 2022](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/b347/live/3bdbd890-9bdc-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Nick Kyrgios (right) and good friend Thanasi Kokkinakis won the Australian Open men's doubles title in 2022
In 2023, Kyrgios admitted assaulting ex-girlfriend Chiara Passari by pushing her on the pavement during a row in Canberra. The magistrate called the incident "a single act of stupidity or frustration" when sparing him a criminal record.
Then two years ago he publicly distanced himself from controversial influencer Andrew Tate, who is currently fighting extradition to the UK on charges including rape and offences related to sex trafficking.
Kyrgios told the BBC he had "deleted posts, unfollowed him and gone to all lengths to distance" himself from Tate.
The current world number 919 will now step away from public life for the next 28 days to "do the work and come back better".
The legal process could take many months - and Kyrgios is no fan of tennis' anti-doping system.

d8acc8fa6c24f07c70128b11.title: Nick Kyrgios: Controversial tennis player's career could be over after positive cocaine test
d8acc8fa6c24f07c70128b11.author: Russell Fuller
d8acc8fa6c24f07c70128b11.content:
![Nick Kyrgios gestures after a point in the Wimbledon men's singles final in 2022](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/71a2/live/4841ebf0-9be2-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Nick Kyrgios has won seven ATP Tour singles titles
- Published
Nick Kyrgios once said there was "zero chance" he would be playing tennis into his 30s.
But it was at the age of 31, while attempting another comeback from serious knee and wrist injuries, that he tested positive for a metabolite of cocaine at June's Mallorca Open.
In a post on social media, Kyrgios said it was a "huge mistake" for which he takes full responsibility.
But he added that recent injuries - he has only played eight tournaments and won two matches since the start of 2023 - have taken a huge toll on him.
"Coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined," he added.
Kyrgios will not be able to play until his case is resolved because of a mandatory provisional suspension.
But although he faces a potential ban of up to four years, his suspension would be limited to a maximum of three months if he can prove the drug was taken out of competition.
Kyrgios suspended after positive cocaine test
The Australian has achieved more than most on the sporting stage. As a 19-year-old in 2014 he stunned then world number one Rafael Nadal on his Centre Court debut, and finished runner-up at Wimbledon eight years later.
At his best, Kyrgios is a flamboyant and athletic shot-maker with flair, touch and an explosive game.
But he can also be destructive and verbally abusive, and has regularly struggled to sustain the levels of professionalism and abstinence needed for a prolonged stay at the very top.
In 2015, Kyrgios was given a suspended 28-day ban for making lewd remarks about Stan Wawrinka's girlfriend during a match in Montreal.
A year later, he was banned for eight weeks for his behaviour - including a "lack of best effort" - at the Shanghai Masters. This was reduced to three weeks after he agreed to consult a sports psychologist.
2019 was the nadir. Kyrgios was defaulted from a match at the Italian Open for hurling a chair on to the court, and was later fined $113,000 for verbally abusing umpire Fergus Murphy in Cincinnati.
The ATP later issued a suspended 16-week ban for a "pattern of behaviour related to his verbal abuse of officials and/or spectators" over the previous 12 months.
![Nick Kyrgios walks off with the Wimbledon singles runner-up trophy after losing the 2022 final to Novak Djokovic](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/a2d0/live/08e2d5b0-9bdc-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Nick Kyrgios reached his sole Grand Slam singles final at Wimbledon in 2022, losing to Novak Djokovic
Kyrgios described 2019 as the "lowest point of my career" when interviewed for Netflix's Break Point documentary series.
"I was drinking, abusing drugs. I lost my relationship with my family, pushed all my close friends away," he said.
"Being bullied at a young age for being short and fat and brown scarred me for sure."
Kyrgios said he wore a compression sleeve to cover up self-harming scars on his arm and spent time in a psychiatric hospital in London to try and "figure out my problems".
He separately spoke about being forced out of a pub in Wimbledon Village by his agent in the early hours of a match day, and told Louis Theroux in 2024 that he would sometimes have "20 to 30 drinks" before playing the next day.
He has confessed to playing too much basketball - including for an hour before he beat David Ferrer in the 2017 Cincinnati Masters semi-finals - and has often said he has been unable to "dedicate" his life to tennis.
"I just enjoy doing whatever I'm doing," he said.
"I don't eat well. I don't train just for tennis, I train just for a general happy living - I know it sounds ridiculous, but I play a bit of tennis on the side."
![Nick Kyrgios and Thanasi Kokkinakis pose after winning the Australian Open men's doubles title in 2022](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/b347/live/3bdbd890-9bdc-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Nick Kyrgios (right) and good friend Thanasi Kokkinakis won the Australian Open men's doubles title in 2022
In 2023, Kyrgios admitted assaulting ex-girlfriend Chiara Passari by pushing her on the pavement during a row in Canberra. The magistrate called the incident "a single act of stupidity or frustration" when sparing him a criminal record.
Then two years ago he publicly distanced himself from controversial influencer Andrew Tate, who is currently fighting extradition to the UK on charges including rape and offences related to sex trafficking.
Kyrgios told the BBC he had "deleted posts, unfollowed him and gone to all lengths to distance" himself from Tate.
The current world number 919 will now step away from public life for the next 28 days to "do the work and come back better".
The legal process could take many months - and Kyrgios is no fan of tennis' anti-doping system.
Describing the system as "awful," he made clear repeatedly his opinion that both Jannik Sinner and Iga Swiatek received overly lenient bans after their recent high-profile doping cases.
"Sad day for tennis. Fairness in tennis does not exist," Kyrgios wrote after Sinner accepted a three-month ban for testing positive for clostebol.
But if he does decide he wants to continue his career into his 30s, much will rest on the process of which Kyrgios has been so critical.

4bd69219528d2d22a9755b7b.title: 'Beyond human intuition': AI designs chip components 500 times smaller than what engineers could ever imagine
4bd69219528d2d22a9755b7b.author: Fiona Jackson
4bd69219528d2d22a9755b7b.content:
![A close up of a rectangular chip on a gold coin with three boxouts on the right side showing various aspects of the chipd](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/SMkTm2nQsCXdJGJyMJkCLG.jpg) 
Photonic microchips are around the size of a penny. This close-up shows computer-designed nanostructures, wavelength splitters, mode sorters and mirrors, while the illustrations on the left show how the components could be integrated into photonic circuits.
Scientists have successfully shrunk three components used in photonic microchips by up to 500 times, leaving considerably more space for other on-chip functionality. The achievement was made possible with an artificial intelligence (AI) algorithm that generated these tiny designs, which the researchers described as "beyond human intuition."
Whereas conventional microchips use electrons to transmit and process information, photonic microchips utilize particles of light (photons). They can therefore process and transmit data much faster than electronic chips can, because photons can carry information at the speed of light. They also offer higher bandwidth, as different wavelengths can carry distinct data streams, and they lose less energy as heat.
As a result, photonic chips are used where fast, high-bandwidth data transmission is essential, such as in fiber-optic communications, data centers, AI, lidar systems for autonomous vehicles, and quantum computing.
Instead of metal wires, micrometer-wide channels called waveguides direct light across the photonic chip. These chips also contain wavelength splitters, spatial mode sorters and mirrors — all of which are essential for separating and directing different wavelengths and light patterns within a footprint a fraction of the width of a human hair.
In the new study, the scientists used AI-generated designs to fabricate these three components on an ultracompact scale. They published their findings May 28 in the journal Nature Communications.
The newly available on-chip space could allow engineers to "unlock new functionalities" by packing on more components, the researchers wrote in the study. Notably, the work demonstrates that AI can produce boundary-pushing chip designs that are also practical to manufacture.
AI worked backward to generate the component designs
The researchers started by informing the algorithm exactly what they wanted the components to do to the light and by providing certain manufacturing constraints, such as limits on how sharply the nanostructures could curve
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The AI algorithm then worked backward, testing and refining different designs until it found the delicate nanostructures that could achieve the desired result.
"Inverse design lets us define what we want light to do, and the optimization finds a structure that does it, often one no human would have drawn," study first author Toby Bi, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Light, said in a statement. "What is exciting is that the same framework can do three quite different jobs on the same chip: route light by wavelength, sort it by spatial mode, and act as compact mirrors that form on-chip optical cavities."
![A gif showing wavy yellow and purple lines getting darker.](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/DoA8fio9BGt4TnCPpvrvUZ.gif)
The components were designed by an AI algorithm that refined their geometry through iterative optimizations for use in photonic circuits.
Components for photonic chips typically have hand-engineered designs. Engineers start with a tried-and-true design and painstakingly optimize it for new performance parameters. On top of being slow, this method limits the range of device geometries that can be explored.
To improve their components further, the team also opted to create the components out of relatively thick silicon nitride — roughly 400 to 800 nanometers thick, compared with 150 to 400 nanometers for standard silicon — which wastes less light and offers stronger wavelength confinement.
The resulting mirrors, which are about 11 μm long, reflected up to 98.5% of incoming light while blocking unwanted light patterns. When placed in pairs on each side of a waveguide, the light bounced between them over 100 times before escaping, demonstrating the silicon nitride's low losses, the scientists explained.
The wavelength splitter is roughly the size of a single bacterium (approximately 5 μm across), and the spatial mode sorter is marginally larger.
AI-designed chips edge closer to real-world use
While the researchers have successfully demonstrated these compact components individually, they have not combined the components into a complete integrated optical circuit yet. Achieving this will be the next step toward building fully functional photonic chips that harness the increased component density enabled by these designs.
Related stories
- Scientists figured out how to shrink huge ultrafast lasers so they fit on a tiny chip — the 'holy grail' of the field
- Breakthrough in experimental light-powered quantum computers could mean scaling them up is now far more viable
- New wonder material designed by AI is as light as foam but as strong as steel
"These results demonstrate the feasibility of compact, fabrication-error-robust, customised photonic components and pave the way for scalable, high-performance integration in silicon nitride-based photonic systems," the researchers wrote in the study.
In recent years, engineers have begun exploring how AI can be integrated into the semiconductor design and fabrication pipeline. In the past, AI-driven approaches have reduced design cycles from weeks to hours while significantly lowering manufacturing costs.
Some systems can even generate effective chip designs from a 200-word prompt. Google's AlphaChip, a machine learning method that designs chip layouts, has produced "superhuman" floor plans that have been deployed in the tech giant's production AI chips.

Fiona cut her teeth writing human interest stories for global news outlets at the press agency SWNS. She has a Master's degree in Chemistry, an NCTJ Diploma and a cocker spaniel named Sully, who she lives with in Bristol, UK.

d71e6420a10b2667c41396d9.title: Cheadle mental health wards ordered to improve upgraded to 'good'
d71e6420a10b2667c41396d9.author: Lynette Horsburgh
d71e6420a10b2667c41396d9.content:
![A nurse is moving a hospital chair along a corridor while two other nurses attend to paperwork](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1152/cpsprodpb/5e59/live/8480fb90-9b3a-11f1-adfc-97cecc6f1ad1.png)
Inspectors carried out tours of two wards as part of the inspection
- Published
Child and adolescent mental health wards at a Greater Manchester hospital that had been ordered to improve has been rated as "good" by health inspectors.
The Care Quality Commission (CQC) has upgraded the rating of the service at Cheadle Royal Hospital's child and adolescent mental health wards after an inspection in April.
The hospital, run by Affinity Healthcare Limited, provides a range of inpatient mental health services for young people between 11-17 and adults. The inspection followed the receipt of information of concern, the CQC said.
CQC inspectors found the hospital had made necessary improvements and was now only in breach of one regulation related to safe care and treatment.
At the previous inspection, inspectors found five breaches of regulation.
At the time of this latest review, the CQC said there were six young people admitted to the main ward and one young person in long-term segregation on another ward, which was not in general use.
Inspectors carried out a tour of the Woodlands and Featherstone wards as well as the clinic room and the ward seclusion suite.
The CQC upgraded its rating for how responsive and well-led the service was from "required improvement" to "good", and has again rated how effective and caring the service is as good.
The report found:
- Staff treated young people with compassion and kindness, respected their privacy and dignity and involved them and their families in planning their care
- Leaders had a good understanding of how the ward was run and were visible and approachable to both staff and young people
- The ward met people's needs well as staff, managed people's cases effectively, they did not move young people between wards unnecessarily and they supported people to leave hospital as soon as they were well enough to do so
- Staff supported young people with discharge planning, working closely with community teams and commissioners to help them move on to suitable placements.
- Staff assessed young people's physical and mental health needs thoroughly on admission and reviewed their care plans regularly to reflect any changes.
However the inspectors also noted:
- Staff did not always store medicines safely, putting some young people at risk of receiving medicines that were out of date or had not been stored at the correct temperature
- Staff did not always update risk records quickly enough after incidents so important information about a young person's specific risks did not always appear in their care plan
- Some issues with maintenance and infection prevention and control issues in the care environment
The CQC has asked Affinity Healthcare Limited for an action plan in response to the concerns found at this assessment.
The health watchdog's overall rating at Cheadle Royal Hospital has remained the same as "requires improvement".

d71e6420a10b2667c41396d9.summary: The Care Quality Commission (CQC) has upgraded the rating of child and adolescent mental health wards at Cheadle Royal Hospital to 'good' following an inspection in April. Inspectors found that the hospital had addressed most previous concerns, reducing its regulatory breaches from five to one, though minor issues related to medicine storage, risk records, and maintenance remain. Despite the upgraded wards, the hospital's overall rating continues to be 'requires improvement'.
key_points: Cheadle Royal Hospital's child and adolescent mental health wards were upgraded from 'requires improvement' to 'good' by the CQC.
The hospital reduced its regulatory breaches from five down to one concerning safe care and treatment.
Inspectors noted that staff treated young people compassionately and conducted thorough physical and mental health assessments.
Areas of concern included the unsafe storage of some medicines, delayed updates to risk records, and minor maintenance and infection control issues.
The CQC requested an action plan from Affinity Healthcare Limited to address the remaining concerns, while the hospital's overall rating remains 'requires improvement'.

The Care Quality Commission (CQC) has upgraded the rating of the service at Cheadle Royal Hospital's child and adolescent mental health wards after an inspection in April.
The hospital, run by Affinity Healthcare Limited, provides a range of inpatient mental health services for young people between 11-17 and adults. The inspection followed the receipt of information of concern, the CQC said.
CQC inspectors found the hospital had made necessary improvements and was now only in breach of one regulation related to safe care and treatment.
At the previous inspection, inspectors found five breaches of regulation.
At the time of this latest review, the CQC said there were six young people admitted to the main ward and one young person in long-term segregation on another ward, which was not in general use.
Inspectors carried out a tour of the Woodlands and Featherstone wards as well as the clinic room and the ward seclusion suite.
The CQC upgraded its rating for how responsive and well-led the service was from "required improvement" to "good", and has again rated how effective and caring the service is as good.
The report found:
- Staff treated young people with compassion and kindness, respected their privacy and dignity and involved them and their families in planning their care
- Leaders had a good understanding of how the ward was run and were visible and approachable to both staff and young people
- The ward met people's needs well as staff, managed people's cases effectively, they did not move young people between wards unnecessarily and they supported people to leave hospital as soon as they were well enough to do so
- Staff supported young people with discharge planning, working closely with community teams and commissioners to help them move on to suitable placements.
- Staff assessed young people's physical and mental health needs thoroughly on admission and reviewed their care plans regularly to reflect any changes.
However the inspectors also noted:
- Staff did not always store medicines safely, putting some young people at risk of receiving medicines that were out of date or had not been stored at the correct temperature
- Staff did not always update risk records quickly enough after incidents so important information about a young person's specific risks did not always appear in their care plan
- Some issues with maintenance and infection prevention and control issues in the care environment
The CQC has asked Affinity Healthcare Limited for an action plan in response to the concerns found at this assessment.
The health watchdog's overall rating at Cheadle Royal Hospital has remained the same as "requires improvement".

Despite the upgraded wards, the hospital's overall rating continues to be 'requires improvement'.

27381da7e4bf20198df3b656.title: Nearly £300,000 wiped off average house price in central London in 25% slump
27381da7e4bf20198df3b656.author: Nicholas Cecil
27381da7e4bf20198df3b656.content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![The London Question: How do young people feel about renting?](https://cdn.ex.co/transformations-account/production/761715bb-261d-4032-af09-a493a82bd926/73003200-4c00-4900-b000-560057006500/thumbnail-360.webp) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) The drop was a startling 25.4%, from £1,145,000 in June 2025 to £854,000 earlier this summer. ![Stamp duty will become more costly for some home buyers from Tuesday (Daniel Leal-Olivas/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2025/03/31/10/6c0308df3355899fd52187827ccd0de2Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzQzNDk5MzQ2-2.21644533.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) New Prime Minister Andy Burnham has more recently signalled that he may raise taxes on the better off, which would impact most on the capital, to ease the cost of living for millions of other families and fund his plans to rebalance Britain’s economy. Some property experts questioned the scale of the home price drops in the ONS figures, saying they were not seeing such sharp declines. ![

Young people are paying high rents in London for small living spaces

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/04/23/16/2197613868.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) For homes bought with a mortgage in the borough, the average house price was £837,000 in June, down 25.2% from £1,119,000 a year ago. The average price paid by first-time buyers was £766,000 this June, 25.3% lower than the £1,025,000 a year ago. Average prices as of June 2026 in Westminster were: * Detached properties: £3,687,000 * Semi-detached properties: £2,581,000 * Terraced properties: £1,548,000 * Flats and maisonettes: £758,000 Tom Bill, head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, said: “Prices in prime central London have fallen by a quarter over the last decade, primarily due to higher rates of stamp duty but also the ending of non dom status and the fact it has become less attractive to be a landlord. Read More Across London, the average house prices fell by 2.5% in the 12 months to June 2026, compared to a drop of 3.1% in the year to May. In Tower Hamlets, the fall was 13.1% from £526,000 to £457,000, or £69,000. In Islington, the drop was 8.1%, from £733,000 to £673,000, or £60,000. ![LONDON, ENGLAND - MARCH 31: A general view of the railway bridge over Camden Lock on March 31, 2012 in London, England. Camden in North London has been one of the city's cultural centres since the 1960's, and is home to the famous Camden Market. The borough is rich in musical heritage with a variety of theatres, art galleries and world famous musical and comedy venues. (Photo by Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2022/05/11/15/GettyImages-142366941.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) In Camden, the average property price went down 7.1% from £897,000 to £833,000, or £64,000. Average annual house price growth across the UK slowed to 2% in June, from 3% the previous month, to reach £272,000.
27381da7e4bf20198df3b656.summary: Central London experienced a significant 25.4% drop in average house prices, falling from £1,145,000 to £854,000. Other London boroughs such as Tower Hamlets, Islington, and Camden also saw price decreases, while property experts questioned the scale of the ONS figures. Prime central London prices have fallen by a quarter over the last decade due to factors like higher stamp duty and the ending of non-dom status.
key_points: Average house prices in central London slumped by 25.4%, wiping nearly £300,000 off the average price.
First-time buyers in the borough paid an average of £766,000 in June, down 25.3% from the previous year.
Other boroughs also recorded declines, including Tower Hamlets down 13.1%, Islington down 8.1%, and Camden down 7.1%.
Experts attribute prime central London's long-term price falls to higher stamp duty, the ending of non-dom status, and diminished appeal for landlords.

691344731bd5501480d20d94.title: Hounslow murder investigation launched as woman dies after fire
691344731bd5501480d20d94.author: Jess Warren
691344731bd5501480d20d94.content:
![A general view of Berkley Avenue in Hounslow.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/521/cpsprodpb/7d82/live/7d47bb80-9bf2-11f1-8470-d18257d2d589.png)
A 48-year-old woman died in hospital following a fire at a residential address in Hounslow
- Published
A murder investigation is under way after a 48-year-old woman died in a fire in west London.
Officers were called to a residential address on Berkeley Avenue, Hounslow, at about 01:15 BST on Wednesday following reports of the blaze, the Metropolitan Police said.
Six men and three women were taken to hospital, where the 48-year-old woman died. Another woman, 40, is in a life-threatening condition.
The Met said no arrests had been made but officers believed the fire may have been started deliberately. Det Ch Insp Neil John said: "Our inquiries are progressing at pace as we work to establish the full circumstances surrounding the fire."
John said the force's thoughts were "first and foremost with the victim's family and loved ones at this extremely difficult time, as well as everyone who has been injured".
The remaining seven people have been discharged after receiving treatment for minor injuries.
John said the force understood the incident to be isolated to a residential address, but officers would remain in the area and provide updates as the investigation continues.
A London Ambulance Service spokesperson said: "We were called at 01:18 BST today to reports of a fire on Berkeley Avenue, Hounslow.
"We sent resources to the scene including ambulance crews, a paramedic in a fast-response car, an incident response officer and paramedics from our hazardous area response team.
"We treated nine patients and took them all to hospital."
