54ce33bf8dddb4748795f741.title: Arsenal legend reveals why Liverpool will destroy Arteta's hopes of signing Bradley Barcola
54ce33bf8dddb4748795f741.author: Rob McCarthy
54ce33bf8dddb4748795f741.content:
![Barcola Liverpool Arsenal](https://d2x51gyc4ptf2q.cloudfront.net/content/uploads/2026/06/12123551/F365-Two-Badges-Bradley-Barcola-Arsenal-Liverpool-1320x742.jpg) 
Arsenal legend Emmanuel Petit has revealed why he believes Liverpool will ultimately beat the reigning Premier League champions to the signing of Bradley Barcola this summer, with a deal set to cost well in excess of £100million.
Both clubs remain on the hunt for a new wide player before the window closes on September 1, with exciting PSG and France star Barcola on the radars of the two English powerhouses.
Liverpool have long been considered the frontrunners to sign Barcola, with the 23-year-old poised to leave the French giants due to negotiations over a new contract having stalled.
While Barcola is understood to be keen on a move to Anfield and personal terms have already been agreed, FSG are currently reluctant to meet PSG’s £130million (€151m) asking price.
Arsenal, for their part, have been a little later in showing their interest in Barcola, but are being linked after offloading Leandro Trossard and also preparing to part ways with Gabriel Martinelli.
Petit, however, believes Barcola would be best served by a move to Andoni Iraola’s Liverpool, especially given the impressive start Christos Tzolis has made at Arsenal since summer switch from Club Brugge.
“Arsenal have just signed Christos Tzolis, who has made a big impression so far, he was brilliant in the Community Shield,” Petit told Grosvenor Sport.
“With Martinelli leaving and Trossard no longer at the club, they likely need another option on the left side.
“If they were to bring in Barcola, it would be difficult for both players to secure a spot in the starting eleven.
“That said, I am a huge fan of Barcola. I believe Liverpool need him much more than Arsenal.
“They definitely need to strengthen their wide areas, particularly on the left flank, they have had problems there since the start of last season.”
Petit struggling to see Liverpool in top four
Meanwhile, Petit believes that even if Liverpool win the race to snap up Barcola, Iraola still faces an uphill task to secure the club a top-four finish this season.
The Spaniard swapped Bournemouth for the Merseyside giants following Arne Slot’s exit at the end of last season, but Petit thinks the Reds currently have too many holes in their squad to compete with a top-four spot.
The Frenchman added: “I am still waiting to see Liverpool’s full intent in the transfer market, as they currently appear to be missing key players.
“They have a new manager in Iraola, and adjusting to the scale of Liverpool after Bournemouth is a big transition.
“Liverpool need results immediately.
“Ultimately, I see the top four being Arsenal, Chelsea, Manchester City, and Manchester United. Liverpool may find it tough again this year.”
54ce33bf8dddb4748795f741.summary: Arsenal legend Emmanuel Petit believes Liverpool will win the race to sign PSG winger Bradley Barcola for over £100 million because they need him more than Arsenal, who recently signed Christos Tzolis. While personal terms are reportedly agreed with Liverpool, FSG is currently hesitant to meet PSG's £130 million valuation. Despite predicting Barcola will choose Liverpool, Petit remains doubtful that the club—now managed by Andoni Iraola following Arne Slot's departure—will finish in the Premier League top four.
key_points: Both Arsenal and Liverpool are pursuing PSG and France winger Bradley Barcola, with a potential deal expected to exceed £100 million.
Barcola has already agreed personal terms with Liverpool, but FSG is reluctant to meet PSG's £130 million asking price.
Emmanuel Petit believes Barcola is better suited to Liverpool because Arsenal recently signed Christos Tzolis, creating potential competition for the starting eleven.
Petit predicts that Arsenal, Chelsea, Manchester City, and Manchester United will make the top four, leaving Liverpool struggling under new manager Andoni Iraola.

“If they were to bring in Barcola, it would be difficult for both players to secure a spot in the starting eleven.
“That said, I am a huge fan of Barcola. I believe Liverpool need him much more than Arsenal.
“They definitely need to strengthen their wide areas, particularly on the left flank, they have had problems there since the start of last season.”
Petit struggling to see Liverpool in top four
Meanwhile, Petit believes that even if Liverpool win the race to snap up Barcola, Iraola still faces an uphill task to secure the club a top-four finish this season.
The Spaniard swapped Bournemouth for the Merseyside giants following Arne Slot’s exit at the end of last season, but Petit thinks the Reds currently have too many holes in their squad to compete with a top-four spot.
The Frenchman added: “I am still waiting to see Liverpool’s full intent in the transfer market, as they currently appear to be missing key players.
“They have a new manager in Iraola, and adjusting to the scale of Liverpool after Bournemouth is a big transition.
“Liverpool need results immediately.
“Ultimately, I see the top four being Arsenal, Chelsea, Manchester City, and Manchester United. Liverpool may find it tough again this year.”

Despite predicting Barcola will choose Liverpool, Petit remains doubtful that the club—now managed by Andoni Iraola following Arne Slot's departure—will finish in the Premier League top four.

d6f9c54254723a88dc2fcea7.title: Rescue mission can’t prevent NASA observatory from falling to Earth | CNN
d6f9c54254723a88dc2fcea7.author: Ashley Strickland
d6f9c54254723a88dc2fcea7.content:
A satellite called LINK that recently launched to boost the orbit of a falling space observatory won’t be able to carry out its daring rescue mission after all.
NASA’s decades-old Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is steadily losing altitude and in danger of reentering Earth’s atmosphere. Designed by Arizona-based Katalyst Space Technologies to save the observatory, the LINK satellite began to encounter difficulty in late July. Just weeks after LINK lifted off on July 3, it started to spin out of control.
Katalyst was able to regain control of the satellite, but the company acknowledged that the issue cost it time, which would delay LINK’s rendezvous with Swift by about a month. However, that postponement — at least initially — did not seem to be a deterrent to the mission.
Now, NASA and Katalyst have announced that LINK’s mission will not capture and boost Swift to a higher orbit “due to ongoing attitude control issues,” according to statements Wednesday.
![LINK launched on July 3 aboard a Northrop Grumman Pegasus XL rocket affixed to the bottom of the company’s Stargazer aircraft.](https://media.cnn.com/api/v1/images/stellar/prod/ne201469-3000x1865.jpg?c=original&q=w_860,c_fill)
Swift’s science mission will come to an end as the observatory likely burns up in Earth’s atmosphere later this year, according to NASA.
“NASA should be willing to move quickly and take smart risks when the potential return is worth it, and that is exactly what we did with this mission,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement.
“This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting. The team moved with extraordinary speed to give Swift a chance to carry out more science while advancing capabilities America will need for satellite servicing in the future.”
But LINK’s journey isn’t over yet, and the lessons learned could be instrumental for future in-space servicing operations.
Demonstrating future capabilities
The mission team is forging ahead with its plan for LINK to rendezvous with Swift — but as a demonstration rather than a rescue.
“We are going to learn everything we can from LINK’s rendezvous attempt and put those lessons to work on the missions that follow,” Isaacman said.
Originally, LINK was expected to conduct a survey of Swift to determine the best grappling points on the observatory, a step that will likely be part of the satellite’s anticipated rendezvous, though it’s currently unclear when this test will take place.
Swift wasn’t designed to be serviced in space, which means that insights from the demonstration could be used for future missions.
“Katalyst designed, developed, and launched an experimental spacecraft to go after an ambitious mission on an aggressive timeline,” said Ghonhee Lee, CEO of Katalyst Space Technologies, in a statement. “We took on this high-risk, high-reward challenge and are proud of the milestones we reached along the way. We have already learned a tremendous amount, and now our job is to turn those lessons into something durable — building a repeatable playbook to inform future rendezvous and proximity operations and satellite servicing.”
Filling the gap
The Swift Observatory, which has no established observational replacement waiting in the wings, has served as an astrophysics multitool in low-Earth orbit since it launched nearly 22 years ago, quickly pivoting to observe celestial objects and cosmic events.
But atmospheric drag, intensified by solar activity, exerted its forces on the observatory, leading NASA to predict that Swift would reenter Earth’s atmosphere once it dips below an optimal altitude of about 185 miles (300 kilometers) above Earth.
Katalyst designed, built, tested and launched LINK in nine months. The robotic satellite lifted off on a Northrop Grumman Pegasus XL rocket, which was released midair by the company’s modified L-1011 aircraft, Stargazer.
Before the satellite’s launch, members of the Swift and LINK teams both acknowledged that the path to boosting the observatory was full of risks that could cause the mission to fail.
“We were all hoping for more science from Swift,” said Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA headquarters in Washington, DC. “But we knew the takeaways from this mission would be worthwhile either way, and we have gained so much through the series of accomplishments up to this point.”
The agency will rely on the rest of its fleet of active observatories to fill Swift’s gap and “will continue to prioritize finding new options to react rapidly to cosmic events,” according to NASA.
“Building, testing, and operating this mission has already strengthened America’s space industry pipeline, advancing in-space servicing capabilities in completely new ways,” Domagal-Goldman said. “NASA is committed to supporting our commercial vendors as they take on difficult tasks with the agency, to push the boundaries of what’s possible.”

Although the satellite encountered trouble and began spinning out of control shortly after its July 3 launch, the mission will still proceed as a rendezvous demonstration. Consequently, the Swift Observatory will likely burn up in Earth's atmosphere later this year, ending its nearly 22-year mission.

LINK experienced attitude control issues and began spinning out of control in late July, delaying its schedule.
NASA and Katalyst announced that LINK can no longer capture and boost Swift, canceling the rescue mission.
The LINK spacecraft will still attempt a rendezvous with Swift as a technology demonstration to aid future in-space servicing operations.
Without a replacement observatory waiting, Swift's science mission will end when it reenters Earth's atmosphere later this year.

c43686efa0945841aec4a542.title: The blood pressure mistakes cardiologists wish you’d stop making
c43686efa0945841aec4a542.author: Ella Nunn
c43686efa0945841aec4a542.content:
![Prof Tony Heagerty in his office](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/15/TELEMMGLPICT000451735395_17841049377242_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqe8exRwkrG0gUQzS_A7vs-NHhMh81Y8GqX3ipA8YMo0k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Prof Tony Heagerty in his office](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/15/TELEMMGLPICT000451735395_17841049377242_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqe8exRwkrG0gUQzS_A7vs-NHhMh81Y8GqX3ipA8YMo0k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
High blood pressure is one of medicine’s greatest paradoxes. It is among the leading preventable risk factors for heart disease, stroke and premature death worldwide, yet it rarely causes symptoms. As a result, many people do not realise they have the condition until it has already begun damaging the blood vessels supplying the heart, brain and kidneys.
Around one in three adults in the UK – an estimated 16 million people – have high blood pressure, and many are completely unaware of it.
The encouraging news is that there is plenty we can do to reduce our risk and keep our blood pressure under control. Here, five leading cardiologists share the most common blood pressure mistakes they see in midlife – and the simple changes that can make a real difference.
Ignoring heavy snoring
Normally, both blood pressure and heart rate fall by around 10 to 20 per cent during sleep. Known as the “nocturnal dip”, this gives the heart and blood vessels a chance to rest and recover overnight.
However, heavy snoring or obstructive sleep apnoea interrupts this recovery process. “The muscles in the throat relax too much, blocking the airway and depriving the body of oxygen, causing repeated awakenings throughout the night and preventing this normal overnight blood pressure dip,” says Dr Teresa Castiello, consultant cardiologist and founder of MIAL Healthcare.
![A portrait of Dr Teresa Castiello, consultant cardiologist and founder of MIAL Healthcare](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/14/TELEMMGLPICT000495192097_17840403072761_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq4GoSUj5tx--cOXjJHDSbw2mfEaXzUGjZTlLbjM4Zpow.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“When blood pressure and heart rate remain elevated overnight, it can increase the risk of high blood pressure and other health issues including heart failure and even dementia,” she explains.
If you or your partner snores heavily, it’s worth getting it checked rather than dismissing it as an inevitable part of ageing. Obstructive sleep apnoea is often highly treatable with airway devices such as CPAP (Continuous Positive Airway Pressure) machines and lifestyle measures including weight loss and, for some people, changing sleep position.
Treating sleep apnoea consistently can help lower blood pressure and reduce strain on the cardiovascular system over time.
Only checking your blood pressure at weekends
Many of us are familiar with “white coat syndrome”, when blood pressure temporarily spikes because of anxiety in the GP’s office. It’s why doctors often advise measuring blood pressure at home over several days, to build a more accurate picture of cardiovascular health.
But if you only reach for the monitor when you’re relaxed at the weekend or at the end of the day, you could be missing stress-related rises in blood pressure during the working week.
“Some people develop high blood pressure at work or in everyday life when they are stressed, which may not show up at the doctor’s surgery or if they only measure their blood pressure at the weekend or in the evening,” says Dr Ali Khavandi, consultant interventional cardiologist at the Royal United Hospital Bath NHS Foundation Trust.
![Dr Ali Khavandi, a consultant cardiologist at the Royal United Hospital](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/14/TELEMMGLPICT000495192125_17840403099410_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqHqEqWIQYN_HlsJ_HcWHEJEgS7S-ukhk48w-_KmtyACY.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“This weekend-only approach creates a ‘best-case scenario’ measurement, hiding stress-related rises in blood pressure that may otherwise go unnoticed,” he explains. “It prevents you from seeing how your daily job strain impacts your cardiovascular system.”
Because high blood pressure rarely causes symptoms, doctors look for patterns over time rather than relying on isolated readings.
Relying on alcohol to relax
So many of us reach for a glass of wine at the end of a stressful working day, forgetting the impact on our heart health.
“High blood pressure and alcohol are best friends,” says Dr Khavandi. “The relationship between alcohol and blood pressure is dose-dependent, meaning the more you drink the greater the impact,” adds Professor Tony Heagerty, honorary consultant physician at Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, where he runs a hypertension service. “It’s also a risk factor for stroke, independent of its effects on blood pressure.”
![A portrait of Prof Tony Heagerty, honorary consultant physician at Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/15/TELEMMGLPICT000451735504_17841049376101_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Some studies suggest that even moderate alcohol consumption may contribute to small rises in blood pressure over time in some people. If you drink more than two alcoholic drinks a day, halving your intake can produce clinically meaningful reductions in blood pressure, with the greatest benefit seen among heavier drinkers, according to research published in The Lancet.
“If you find yourself reaching for alcohol as a way to relax, try experimenting with other ways to switch off,” Prof Heagerty advises, “whether that is taking a long bath, going for a walk, or cooking a new recipe”.
Thinking exercise makes you immune
In her clinic, Dr Castiello recalls shocked patients saying: “But doctor, I am highly active, I eat exceptionally well, I do yoga – how can my blood pressure be an issue?” She says: “This highlights the misconception that hypertension is exclusively a third-age affliction or something that only affects sedentary individuals.”
In reality, ageing itself – alongside age-related hormonal changes, including the menopause in women and declining testosterone levels in some men – can contribute to rising blood pressure, even among people who are otherwise healthy and active. A healthy lifestyle still helps, Dr Castiello stresses, but at these transition points, it isn’t always enough on its own.
“Oestrogen naturally helps keep blood vessels flexible and dilated,” explains Dr Nabila Laskar, consultant cardiologist and specialist in cardiac imaging at St Bartholomew’s Hospital. “As its levels decline during menopause, blood vessels can become stiffer and less able to relax, leading to higher blood pressure.”
![Dr Nabila Laskar, consultant cardiologist and specialist in cardiac imaging at St Bartholomew's Hospital](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/15/TELEMMGLPICT000495329297_17841272780770_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqOfbQuL7vt0ioTIEx8Tqi0Ad_otF3axIcGgYHqpm5-IA.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“Reducing the salt in your diet, maintaining a healthy weight and walking at a brisk pace for at least 150 minutes per week can all help to manage this risk,” Dr Laskar says.
Shrugging off “borderline” blood pressure
While it’s tempting to shrug off a slightly elevated reading as “fine”, you do so at your peril, says Dr Castiello: “This is a dangerous and pervasive myth”.
While a clinic reading of 125/85 mmHg isn’t considered hypertension, it does not mean you are risk-free. “Slightly elevated readings can still signal an increased long-term risk of cardiovascular disease, particularly when combined with other factors such as age, family history, smoking, excess weight or diabetes,” explains Dr Gosia Wamil, consultant cardiologist at Mayo Clinic Healthcare and The Manor Hospital.
The latest European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines, published in 2024, introduced a new category of “elevated blood pressure”, covering clinic readings between 120-139 mmHg systolic or 70-89 mmHg diastolic. This differs from current UK NICE guidance, which uses different thresholds and recommends confirming hypertension with home or ambulatory monitoring. Meanwhile, in the UK, an average home blood pressure reading of 135/85 mmHg or higher is considered high.
![Dr Gosia Wamil, consultant cardiologist at Mayo Clinic Healthcare and The Manor Hospital](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/15/TELEMMGLPICT000495297892_17841049354400_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqT1yghX8zbx7fxQBY89c64Yh-1OKnoApjyaprnWnv9tw.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The good news is that this stage offers an opportunity to act. Improving your diet, exercising regularly, maintaining a healthy weight and reducing alcohol intake can all help prevent blood pressure from rising further and reduce future cardiovascular risk.
Missing the salt hiding in everyday foods
When we think of salty foods, most of us know the obvious culprits: bacon, crisps, takeaways and adding salt at the table. But plenty of everyday foods – including those with a healthy reputation – can also contain surprising amounts of salt, says Dr Wamil.
Canned soups, wholemeal bread, breakfast cereals, some low-fat cheeses – including feta and reduced-fat cheddar – and smoked fish such as kippers and smoked salmon can all contain significant amounts of sodium, which is the main component of salt. Manufacturers often add it to preserve food and enhance flavour.
A typical serving of smoked salmon can provide around 1.5 to 2g of salt – roughly 30 per cent of the recommended maximum daily intake of 6g for an adult.
Over time, eating too much salt can “cause the body to retain more water, increasing total blood volume and forcing the heart to work harder to pump blood while simultaneously stiffening blood vessel walls”, Dr Wamil says.
The best way to manage this risk is to pay closer attention to the foods you eat regularly. UK guidance recommends that adults consume no more than 6g of salt a day (around one teaspoon). Check food labels, choose fresh or frozen whole foods where possible, and look for products labelled “low salt”, “low sodium” or “no added salt”.
Forgetting the damage it can do to your brain
Many people think of high blood pressure as a problem that mainly affects the heart. But persistent hypertension can also take a toll on the brain, increasing the risk of stroke, cognitive decline and dementia.
Dr Khavandi compares undiagnosed high blood pressure to “leaving a tap on and letting it drip in the background for a long period”. Over time, this constant pressure can silently damage the small blood vessels that supply the brain.
“This vascular damage contributes to vascular dementia and is associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease,” he explains. While some of this damage may be irreversible, the good news is that controlling blood pressure can significantly reduce the risk of stroke and is associated with a lower risk of cognitive decline over time.
Ultimately, the advice remains reassuringly simple: maintain a healthy weight, stay physically active, eat a balanced diet, limit salt and alcohol, prioritise good sleep and have your blood pressure checked regularly.
c43686efa0945841aec4a542.summary: High blood pressure is a major, often symptomless risk factor for heart disease, stroke, and dementia, affecting millions of adults who remain unaware of it. Leading cardiologists highlight several common mistakes people make regarding their blood pressure in midlife, such as ignoring heavy snoring, only testing on weekends, relying on alcohol to relax, and overlooking hidden salt in everyday foods. Making simple lifestyle adjustments and monitoring blood pressure consistently can significantly reduce cardiovascular and cognitive risks over time.
key_points: Ignoring heavy snoring or sleep apnoea prevents the normal overnight drop in blood pressure, increasing long-term cardiovascular risks.
Checking blood pressure only on relaxed weekends can hide stress-related spikes that occur during the working week.
Regularly relying on alcohol to relax contributes to dose-dependent increases in blood pressure and stroke risk.
Being active and healthy does not make individuals immune to hypertension, as age-related hormonal changes like menopause can cause blood vessels to stiffen.
Everyday foods like bread, breakfast cereals, and canned soups often contain surprising amounts of hidden salt that force the heart to work harder.

![Dr Ali Khavandi, a consultant cardiologist at the Royal United Hospital](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/14/TELEMMGLPICT000495192125_17840403099410_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqHqEqWIQYN_HlsJ_HcWHEJEgS7S-ukhk48w-_KmtyACY.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“This weekend-only approach creates a ‘best-case scenario’ measurement, hiding stress-related rises in blood pressure that may otherwise go unnoticed,” he explains. “It prevents you from seeing how your daily job strain impacts your cardiovascular system.”
Because high blood pressure rarely causes symptoms, doctors look for patterns over time rather than relying on isolated readings.
Relying on alcohol to relax
So many of us reach for a glass of wine at the end of a stressful working day, forgetting the impact on our heart health.
“High blood pressure and alcohol are best friends,” says Dr Khavandi. “The relationship between alcohol and blood pressure is dose-dependent, meaning the more you drink the greater the impact,” adds Professor Tony Heagerty, honorary consultant physician at Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, where he runs a hypertension service. “It’s also a risk factor for stroke, independent of its effects on blood pressure.”
![A portrait of Prof Tony Heagerty, honorary consultant physician at Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/15/TELEMMGLPICT000451735504_17841049376101_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqpVlberWd9EgFPZtcLiMQf0Rf_Wk3V23H2268P_XkPxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Some studies suggest that even moderate alcohol consumption may contribute to small rises in blood pressure over time in some people. If you drink more than two alcoholic drinks a day, halving your intake can produce clinically meaningful reductions in blood pressure, with the greatest benefit seen among heavier drinkers, according to research published in The Lancet.
“If you find yourself reaching for alcohol as a way to relax, try experimenting with other ways to switch off,” Prof Heagerty advises, “whether that is taking a long bath, going for a walk, or cooking a new recipe”.
Thinking exercise makes you immune
In her clinic, Dr Castiello recalls shocked patients saying: “But doctor, I am highly active, I eat exceptionally well, I do yoga – how can my blood pressure be an issue?” She says: “This highlights the misconception that hypertension is exclusively a third-age affliction or something that only affects sedentary individuals.”
In reality, ageing itself – alongside age-related hormonal changes, including the menopause in women and declining testosterone levels in some men – can contribute to rising blood pressure, even among people who are otherwise healthy and active. A healthy lifestyle still helps, Dr Castiello stresses, but at these transition points, it isn’t always enough on its own.
“Oestrogen naturally helps keep blood vessels flexible and dilated,” explains Dr Nabila Laskar, consultant cardiologist and specialist in cardiac imaging at St Bartholomew’s Hospital. “As its levels decline during menopause, blood vessels can become stiffer and less able to relax, leading to higher blood pressure.”
![Dr Nabila Laskar, consultant cardiologist and specialist in cardiac imaging at St Bartholomew's Hospital](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/15/TELEMMGLPICT000495329297_17841272780770_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqOfbQuL7vt0ioTIEx8Tqi0Ad_otF3axIcGgYHqpm5-IA.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
“Reducing the salt in your diet, maintaining a healthy weight and walking at a brisk pace for at least 150 minutes per week can all help to manage this risk,” Dr Laskar says.
Shrugging off “borderline” blood pressure
While it’s tempting to shrug off a slightly elevated reading as “fine”, you do so at your peril, says Dr Castiello: “This is a dangerous and pervasive myth”.
While a clinic reading of 125/85 mmHg isn’t considered hypertension, it does not mean you are risk-free. “Slightly elevated readings can still signal an increased long-term risk of cardiovascular disease, particularly when combined with other factors such as age, family history, smoking, excess weight or diabetes,” explains Dr Gosia Wamil, consultant cardiologist at Mayo Clinic Healthcare and The Manor Hospital.
The latest European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines, published in 2024, introduced a new category of “elevated blood pressure”, covering clinic readings between 120-139 mmHg systolic or 70-89 mmHg diastolic. This differs from current UK NICE guidance, which uses different thresholds and recommends confirming hypertension with home or ambulatory monitoring. Meanwhile, in the UK, an average home blood pressure reading of 135/85 mmHg or higher is considered high.
![Dr Gosia Wamil, consultant cardiologist at Mayo Clinic Healthcare and The Manor Hospital](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/07/15/TELEMMGLPICT000495297892_17841049354400_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqT1yghX8zbx7fxQBY89c64Yh-1OKnoApjyaprnWnv9tw.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The good news is that this stage offers an opportunity to act. Improving your diet, exercising regularly, maintaining a healthy weight and reducing alcohol intake can all help prevent blood pressure from rising further and reduce future cardiovascular risk.
Missing the salt hiding in everyday foods
When we think of salty foods, most of us know the obvious culprits: bacon, crisps, takeaways and adding salt at the table. But plenty of everyday foods – including those with a healthy reputation – can also contain surprising amounts of salt, says Dr Wamil.
Canned soups, wholemeal bread, breakfast cereals, some low-fat cheeses – including feta and reduced-fat cheddar – and smoked fish such as kippers and smoked salmon can all contain significant amounts of sodium, which is the main component of salt. Manufacturers often add it to preserve food and enhance flavour.
A typical serving of smoked salmon can provide around 1.5 to 2g of salt – roughly 30 per cent of the recommended maximum daily intake of 6g for an adult.
Over time, eating too much salt can “cause the body to retain more water, increasing total blood volume and forcing the heart to work harder to pump blood while simultaneously stiffening blood vessel walls”, Dr Wamil says.
The best way to manage this risk is to pay closer attention to the foods you eat regularly. UK guidance recommends that adults consume no more than 6g of salt a day (around one teaspoon). Check food labels, choose fresh or frozen whole foods where possible, and look for products labelled “low salt”, “low sodium” or “no added salt”.
Forgetting the damage it can do to your brain
Many people think of high blood pressure as a problem that mainly affects the heart. But persistent hypertension can also take a toll on the brain, increasing the risk of stroke, cognitive decline and dementia.
Dr Khavandi compares undiagnosed high blood pressure to “leaving a tap on and letting it drip in the background for a long period”. Over time, this constant pressure can silently damage the small blood vessels that supply the brain.
“This vascular damage contributes to vascular dementia and is associated with an increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease,” he explains. While some of this damage may be irreversible, the good news is that controlling blood pressure can significantly reduce the risk of stroke and is associated with a lower risk of cognitive decline over time.
Ultimately, the advice remains reassuringly simple: maintain a healthy weight, stay physically active, eat a balanced diet, limit salt and alcohol, prioritise good sleep and have your blood pressure checked regularly.
d1c2c4e7f1fc57330233009e.summary: High blood pressure is a major, often symptomless risk factor for heart disease, stroke, and dementia, affecting millions of adults who remain unaware of it. Leading cardiologists highlight several common mistakes people make regarding their blood pressure in midlife, such as ignoring heavy snoring, only testing on weekends, relying on alcohol to relax, and overlooking hidden salt in everyday foods. Making simple lifestyle adjustments and monitoring blood pressure consistently can significantly reduce cardiovascular and cognitive risks over time.
key_points: Ignoring heavy snoring or sleep apnoea prevents the normal overnight drop in blood pressure, increasing long-term cardiovascular risks.
Checking blood pressure only on relaxed weekends can hide stress-related spikes that occur during the working week.
Regularly relying on alcohol to relax contributes to dose-dependent increases in blood pressure and stroke risk.
Being active and healthy does not make individuals immune to hypertension, as age-related hormonal changes like menopause can cause blood vessels to stiffen.
Everyday foods like bread, breakfast cereals, and canned soups often contain surprising amounts of hidden salt that force the heart to work harder.

bfdb2de6d4711ae97596038b.title: London Playbook PM: Rough around the pledges
bfdb2de6d4711ae97596038b.author: Emilio Casalicchio
bfdb2de6d4711ae97596038b.content:
Good afternoon. This is Emilio Casalicchio.
WEDNESDAY CHEAT SHEET
— Andy Burnham admitted government funding might not solve the rough sleeping crisis as he called on others to help.
— The PM confirmed a chunk of his No.10 wages will also go to the homelessness cause.
— Nigel Farage argued the pledge to house rough sleepers will attract asylum seekers.
— The government is open to discussing the tech giant tax that Donald Trump hates.
— Westminster just became a Lib Dem target seat.
TOP OF THE NEWSLIST
ROUGH AROUND THE PLEDGES: Andy Burnham admitted government cash might not be enough to end rough sleeping this Christmas — but he urged others to help as part of a national mission.
Rough estimate: “This is now a call,” he told broadcasters in a TV clip this afternoon during his visit to the Changing Lives homelessness charity in Newcastle to promote his new scheme. “The government money may not fully get us there. I’m saying to wider society, faith organizations: let’s see if we can do this together. Let’s see if Britain can do this.”
The emotional appeal: “As prime minister I want to waste no time in making those moves to say no, this is who we are, this is how we should be, nobody should sleep rough on the streets of Britain,” he added.
How the PM is contributing direct: Burnham confirmed to the Big Issue this afternoon he will give 15 percent of his prime ministerial wage to help tackle homelessness — on top of the already-announced 15 percent of his income as an MP. “I wouldn’t want to ask anybody to do anything that I’m not prepared to do,” he told the magazine. “I want to lead from the front.”
But but but: Burnham was forced to defend his record leading from the front as mayor of Greater Manchester, where his efforts to end rough sleeping saw an initial fall in numbers before they rose again. He said the scheme attracted homeless people from other areas with less support.
As such: “The only way to achieve ‘everyone in’ is everywhere doing it,” he said in his clip. “We can do this, but only if all areas are pulling in the same direction.” Communities Secretary Angela Rayner told Sky the “lesson from Greater Manchester is it’s really difficult to do in isolation.”
And so it follows … that Reform reckons the offer of free homes will drive more asylum seekers to Britain — as it attracted more rough sleepers to Manchester. “Everything for free if you come by boat,” was how Nigel Farage put it.
Another rough ride: “Andy Burnham promised to end rough sleeping in Manchester, and failed because he didn’t do the hard work necessary,” Shadow Housing Secretary James Cleverly said. Although bear in mind the Tories pledged to end rough sleeping before 2024 but instead oversaw a 95 percent increase (according to the official snapshot estimate in 2025) in half a decade.
More enthusiastic: Homelessness charities welcomed the Burnham announcement (natch.) Labour MP Danny Beales (who was made homeless twice as a teenager) is on LBC in the next hour to champion the plan.
**Can Europe still win on the decisive issues? Join the debate on “How Europe Wins” and engage with leading voices from politics, science, business, and culture at the European Forum Alpbach from 24 August to 4 September. Secure your ticket now!**
DRIVETIME DEBRIEF
COULD BE A BIG DEAL: The Burnham administration is willing to chat through American angst about the U.K. digital services tax, my POLITICO tech colleague Joe Bambridge reports. “We remain open to discussing U.S. concerns and working with partners internationally,” a spokesperson told Joe — a softening on the long-held position that the tax is set in stone. The spokesperson made the comments after U.S. trade official Jamieson Greer told the Times White House threats to take action against the tax are “not a bluff.”
On an unrelated (?) note … AI minister Kanishka Naryan has been in the U.S. chatting with counterparts.
PRICE OF WAR: The Tories heaped the blame on Labour after inflation rose to 2.9 percent in the 12 months to July — up from 2.6 percent in the 12 months to June. The main driver for the price hikes was rocketing gas prices as a result of Donald Trump’s war with Iran.
On which note … net zero department PPS Jeevun Sandher said the Tories bigging up fossil fuels during a gas price rollercoaster is “weird” and attacked Shadow Energy Secretary Claire Coutinho for failing to account for price shocks in her big pitch against net zero. She hit back to note that her price forecast numbers are based on official departmental data, adding, for good measure: “These people are absolute clowns.” But Sandher pointed out that the departmental forecasts also do not account for Trump-shaped shocks.
Wanting to get in on the action: Reform published a list of all the times Coutinho backed net zero and championed green measures while she was energy secretary. At her press conference this morning she argued Reform “think they can just say ‘net stupid zero,’ and that’s a plan. It isn’t.” Coutinho told our energy reporter Nick Earl that she asked her previous department to “interrogate” assumptions about net zero, and decided “they didn’t have the evidence.”
Now hear this: Coutinho is on LBC in the next hour, while Lib Dem Leader Ed Davey (who was making a similar point to Sandher about gas prices) is on the Radio 4 PM show. He’ll also be talking about his proposal to take part in an EU scheme to tackle the small boats issue.
GIVE AND TAKE: Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden urged Reform to state what they would be willing to give Brussels in exchange for excluding EU settled status citizens from most welfare schemes, as Robert Jenrick pledged this week. “Those parties who suggest they want to do this should be clear that they’re going to plunge us back into the kind of negotiations that we were in for several years after the Brexit referendum, and there would be a price for any change,” McFadden told LBC’s Bethany Dawson.
HR NOTE: Private Eye reckons the reason outspoken MP Karl Turner hasn’t got the Labour whip back (despite his claims Andy Burnham would soon reinstate it) is because party bosses want him to apologize to former Chief Whip Jonathan Reynolds. Turner has been accusing Reynolds of orchestrating “hostile briefings” about his mental health, and is even threatening legal action. But Reynolds insists the briefings were nothing to do with him.
NICE WORK, IF YOU CAN RETIRE FROM IT: Private Eye also notes that former senior Treasury official Sam Beckett received more than £300,000 on retirement from her £170,000 position in January — on top of her pension arrangements. HMT told the mag the sum (detailed in the latest departmental annual report) was “in line with civil service compensation scheme rules and established guidelines.”
Speaking of pensions: Last one from Private Eye, which reports Capita won a £9 million extension to its contract managing pensions for the Environment Agency … despite its ongoing public sector pensions debacle (see here and here.)
MEDIA NEWS: More than 50 MPs have written to the press regulator demanding an investigation into the coverage of academic Jason Arday, who died following a plagiarism row. Full list here — and PoliticsHome has a writeup.
SOCIAL (MEDIA) AFFAIRS
NAKED RAGE BAIT: “I am officially giving up on the difference between less and fewer,” Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant wrote on social media. At least that’s one less grammar pedant to contend with.
BEYOND THE M25
ON THE RAILS: The Department for Transport is reassuring passengers that the U.K.’s railways are “amongst the safest in the world” after the Rail Accident Investigation Branch found a track “irregularity” near where a train was derailed in Lewes last week. The BBC has more.
SHOWDOWN: Here’s another reminder that Michael Marra and Joe Fagan will take part in a televised debate at 10.45pm on STV — nine days before members can vote on the next Scottish Labour leader. Since getting on the ballot, the pair have been setting out their stalls and Marra today called for all parties in Holyrood to agree a set of proposals to reduce child poverty.
CASE OPEN: The IDF ordered a criminal investigation into the death of 5-year-old Hind Rajab, who was killed by Israel’s military in January 2024. It is one of only two cases on which military prosecutors have been instructed to take action, according to the FT.
IN FRANCE: A former senior French civil servant stands accused of drugging interviewees during job interviews. Christian Nègre is suspected of administering diuretics to almost 200 women. The BBC interviewed two of his accusers.
TONIGHT’S MEDIA ROUND
LEADING THE NEWS BULLETINS: Channel 5 News (5 p.m.) leads on the drownings of three family members in West Sussex.
Tom Swarbrick at Drive (LBC, until 6 p.m.): Labour MP Danny Beales … Tory ex-West Midlands Mayor Andy Street … Shadow Energy Secretary Claire Coutinho.
Drive with Calum MacDonald (Times Radio, until 7 p.m.): Crossbench peer John Bird … Labour MP Tom Rutland.
Kevin O’Sullivan (Talk, until 7 p.m.): Labour MP Graham Stringer.
BBC PM (Radio 4, 5 p.m.): Lib Dem Leader Ed Davey.
GB News Tonight (GB News, 7 p.m.): Former Chancellor Kwasi Kwarteng.
The Evening Edition with Darryl Morris (Times Radio, 7 p.m.): Danny Beales.
Peter Cardwell’s Evening Exchange (Talk, 7 p.m.): Crossbench peer Polly Neate.
Jacob Rees-Mogg’s State of the Nation (GB News, 8 p.m.): Nigel Garage ally Arron Banks … Claire Coutinho.
Patrick Christys Tonight (GB News, 9 p.m.): Popular Conservatism Director Mark Littlewood … Reform UK councilor Jaymey McIvor.
Newsnight (BBC 2, 10.30 p.m.): Labour peer Shami Chakrabarti and Tory ex-West Midlands Mayor Andy Street.
REVIEWING THE PAPERS TONIGHT: Sky News (10 p.m.): The Times’ Aubrey Allegretti and broadcaster Daisy McAndrew … Times Radio (10.30 p.m.): Journalist Laura Trevelyan and Former Downing Street comms director Jonathan Haslam.
**Playbook came to Brussels in 2015 and changed how this town starts its day. It has now landed in Canberra: a capital with just as many officials and, until now, no daily briefing of its own. Canberra Playbook: free, daily, radically impartial. Subscribe free.**
TOMORROW’S WORLD
THE END RESULT: Expect an education minister doing interviews about GCSE and vocational qualification results.
CLASS DISRUPTORS: Reform education spokesperson Suella Braverman will also be talking results alongside Richard Tice at a press conference in Enfield from 11 a.m.
WHAT THE GOVERNMENT WANTS TO TALK ABOUT: Andy Burnham is expected to be out and about talking about waste crime, while the transport department is talking about train drivers.
ANY OTHER BUSINESS
HAPPY TO CLARIFY: The Whitehall audit of press officers while Boris Johnson was prime minister was launched before the Covid pandemic.
WESTMINSTER JUST BECAME A LIB DEM TARGET SEAT: The Gail’s on Victoria Street is now open. H/t the Speccie’s James Heale. A Lib Dem official said: “Operation Cinnamon Bun is so back.”
PACKED LUNCH OR PALACE LUNCH: It’s recess! Make the most of a quiet parliament with a wander around to check out the menus.
ON THIS DAY IN POLITICS: On Aug. 19, 2005 former Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam, who was integral to the peace process, died aged 55. More from the Tides of History account on Instagram here.
WRITING PLAYBOOK TOMORROW MORNING: Caroline Hug.
THANKS TO: My editor Matt Honeycombe-Foster, reporter Isabel Loubser and the POLITICO production team for making it look nice.

PACKED LUNCH OR PALACE LUNCH: It’s recess! Make the most of a quiet parliament with a wander around to check out the menus.

1d1fbe66e24206be2b58757f.summary: Andy Burnham admitted that government funding alone may not end the rough sleeping crisis and called on wider society to help, while confirming he will donate a portion of his wages to the cause. Meanwhile, the government signaled it is open to discussing U.S. concerns regarding the digital services tax. Additionally, inflation rose to 2.9 percent largely driven by gas prices connected to Donald Trump's conflict with Iran.
key_points: Andy Burnham acknowledged government funding might be insufficient to solve rough sleeping and urged societal participation.
The government expressed openness to discussing U.S. concerns surrounding the U.K. digital services tax.
U.K. inflation increased to 2.9 percent in the 12 months to July, driven by rising gas prices linked to the Iran conflict.
Reform UK argued that pledges to house rough sleepers would attract more asylum seekers to Britain.
